title: Why saving files isn't enough
description: Ctrl+S saves what's on disk right now. It doesn't save a version you can get back to — version control is a second, deliberate system for that, and it's not the same thing as backup.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why overwriting a file with Ctrl+S destroys the previous version
Identify why manual versioning schemes (renamed files, backup folders) break down on real projects
State what a version control system tracks that a saved file alone doesn't

contentSections.title: Ctrl+S only remembers the last version

contentSections.body: You've been rewriting a function for two hours. It's worse now than it was at the start, and you have no idea which of your last six saves actually had it working. You hit Ctrl+Z a dozen times, but you closed and reopened the file an hour ago, so undo history is gone too. The version that worked is gone — not hidden somewhere, gone.

contentSections.scenario:
Four ways people try to protect themselves from this before they've heard of version control:

1. Rename the file to `script_v2.js`, then `script_v2_final.js`, then `script_v2_final_ACTUALLY.js`
2. Keep a `backup/` folder and copy the whole project into it before making risky changes
3. Email the file to themselves as an attachment before editing
4. Just keep hitting Ctrl+S and hope for the best
contentSections.question: All four of these are real, common habits. Which problem do all four of them share?

options.label: They all only capture a version if you remember to do it, and none of them explain why a version was made
They're all too slow to actually do while coding
They only work for JavaScript files, not other languages

feedback.manual: Right. Every one of these depends on you remembering to do it, right before the moment you'd actually need it — which is exactly the moment you don't yet know you'll need it. And even when you do remember, "script_v2_final_ACTUALLY.js" tells future-you nothing about what changed or why. You get a pile of near-identical files with no record of the reasoning.
feedback.slow: Speed isn't really the issue — copying a folder takes seconds. The real problem is that all four depend on you remembering to do them at the right moment, and even when you do, none of them record *why* a version exists.
feedback.language: None of these four techniques care what language the file is written in — the problem isn't language-specific. It's that all four are manual, memory-dependent, and leave no explanation of what changed.

contentSections.concept: Manual versioning schemes share the same failure mode: they only capture a version if a human remembers to, at the exact moment they'd need to remember to — and even then, a filename or a folder copy carries no explanation of what changed or why. Version control (git) makes recording a version a first-class, deliberate action with a required explanation attached, and keeps the entire history searchable, not just the last copy you happened to make.

contentSections.body: There's a second, separate problem underneath this: Ctrl+S doesn't create a new version — it *overwrites* the old one. The file on disk is only ever the single most recent state. Once you save over a working version with a broken one, the working version isn't in a backup somewhere waiting for you; it's gone, unless something else was deliberately keeping a copy. Version control (we'll use git, the one almost everyone actually uses) exists specifically to be that something else — recording a full snapshot of your project every time you tell it to, each one labeled with a message explaining what changed and why, and every one of them recoverable later, not just the last one.
Ctrl+S overwrites; it doesn't version. Version control is a separate, deliberate system for keeping — and explaining — every state you actually want to be able to return to.

contentSections.title: Saving to disk doesn't tell git anything

contentSections.body: You install git, run one setup command, and go back to coding. You save your file the normal way — Ctrl+S, like always. Does git now know something changed?

contentSections.question: You have a git-tracked project open. You edit a file and press Ctrl+S. Does git automatically record this as a new version?
contentSections.hint: Git isn't a background process quietly watching your keystrokes — it only acts when you tell it to.
contentSections.answer: No. Saving a file changes what's on disk, but git does nothing on its own — it has no idea a save even happened until you explicitly ask it to look. Git can tell you a file has *changed since the last version it recorded* (that's `git status`), but it will never record a new version by itself. Recording one is always a deliberate, two-step action you take on purpose — covered next lesson.

contentSections.body: This is the mental model worth keeping from lesson one: your project, on disk, is the *working directory* — whatever you're actively editing, right now, unversioned. Git separately keeps a *history* of snapshots you've explicitly asked it to save. The two are connected but distinct: editing and saving changes the working directory; only a deliberate git action adds to the history. Nothing you do with your editor's normal Save touches that history at all — which is exactly why version control has to be learned as its own skill, not assumed to happen automatically.
Git only records what you explicitly tell it to record. Editing and saving a file never does that by itself.

title: Commits: snapshots with a message that explains why
description: A commit is a saved snapshot of your whole project plus a message explaining the change. Staging is the step in between — choosing exactly what goes into that snapshot.

learningObjectives.text: Run the stage-then-commit sequence to record a new snapshot
Write a commit message that explains why a change was made, not just what changed
Explain what staging lets you do that committing everything at once doesn't

contentSections.title: A commit message is a note to future you

contentSections.body: Three months from now, something in your project breaks. You run a tool that shows you which commit introduced the broken line. The commit message reads: "fixed stuff". That commit touched four files. You're no closer to understanding what happened than before you looked.

contentSections.scenario:
Two commit messages for the same actual change — fixing a bug where the date picker crashed when nothing was selected:

A) "fixed stuff"
B) "Fix: date picker crashed on empty selection — guard against null before formatting"
contentSections.question: Three months from now, searching your project's history for why a specific line changed, which message actually helps?

options.label: B — it names the bug, the trigger, and the fix, so it means something without opening the code
A — it's shorter, so it's faster to read in a long history
Neither — you'd have to read the actual code change either way, so the message doesn't matter

feedback.b: Right. "fixed stuff" is technically a message, but it carries zero information — it could describe almost any commit in the project's history. B tells you what broke, what condition triggered it, and what the fix actually was, all without opening a single file. That's the entire value of a commit message: making the history searchable by what happened, not just when.
feedback.a: Shorter isn't better if it says nothing. "fixed stuff" is fast to read and fast to be useless — you'll still have to open the diff to find out what it means, which defeats the point of having a message at all.
feedback.neither: The message is often the fastest way to find the right commit in the first place — searching a hundred commits for "date picker" or "null" only works if the messages actually contain real words describing the change. A vague message means you're stuck opening every candidate commit by hand.

contentSections.concept: A commit message's job is to explain *why* a change happened, in words specific enough that future-you (or anyone else) can find and understand it without re-reading the diff. "Fixed stuff", "updates", and "wip" all fail this — they're true, but they carry no information a search or a skim can use.

contentSections.body:
A commit itself is a full snapshot of your project at that moment, permanently recorded in the project's history, tagged with the message you write for it. Making one is two commands run from the terminal, inside your project folder:

```
git add .
git commit -m "Fix: date picker crashed on empty selection"
```

`git add .` stages every changed file — more on exactly what "staging" means in a moment. `git commit -m "..."` takes what's staged and permanently records it as a new snapshot, with your message attached. From that point on, that exact state of your project is recoverable, forever, by that commit.
`git add .` then `git commit -m "..."` records a snapshot — and the message is what makes that snapshot findable and meaningful later.

contentSections.title: Staging: choosing what goes in the snapshot

contentSections.body: You've been working for an hour. You fixed a genuine bug in the login form, and separately, you started sketching out a new feature that's half-finished and not ready to commit yet. `git add .` would stage both. Do you have to commit them together?

contentSections.problem: You've changed two unrelated files: `login.js` (a real, finished bug fix) and `newFeature.js` (a half-built experiment you're not ready to commit). You want one clean commit for the bug fix only, leaving the experiment untouched on disk but out of the snapshot.

steps.label: Check what's changed
steps.work: git status
steps.why: Shows every file that differs from the last commit — here, both login.js and newFeature.js, listed as modified/untracked.

steps.label: Stage only the finished file
steps.work: git add login.js
steps.why: Staging is selective — you name exactly which file(s) join the next snapshot. newFeature.js is left alone entirely; it's still on disk, just not part of what's about to be committed.

steps.label: Confirm what's staged
steps.work: git status
steps.why: Now shows login.js staged for commit, and newFeature.js still listed as an unstaged change — a clear check before you commit.

steps.label: Commit only what's staged
steps.work: git commit -m "Fix: login form accepted an empty password"
steps.why: Only login.js becomes part of this snapshot. newFeature.js remains exactly as it was on disk, untouched and uncommitted, ready to be worked on and committed separately once it's actually done.

faded.problem: Same situation, different files: you fixed a real bug in `checkout.js`, and separately have unfinished, half-broken experiments in `pricing-test.js` that you don't want in this commit.

blanks.prompt: First command — see what's changed so far
blanks.why: Always the first move: see the full list of what differs from the last commit before deciding what to do about it.

blanks.prompt: Stage only the finished bug fix, not the experiment
blanks.why: Naming the file explicitly stages only that one — pricing-test.js stays out of the snapshot entirely.

blanks.prompt: Commit with a message that explains the actual fix
blanks.answer: git commit -m "Fix: checkout total didn't include tax on multi-item carts"
blanks.why: A specific message naming the bug and its trigger — not "fixed checkout" — is what makes this findable later.

contentSections.procedure: Stage only the files that belong together as one logical change, confirm with git status, then commit with a message that names the actual problem and fix.

contentSections.body: Staging is the step where you decide exactly what belongs in the next snapshot — it lets you split unrelated changes into separate, honest commits instead of one tangled one.

title: Undoing: the three things you'll actually need
description: Three different undo situations need three different commands: fixing your last commit before anyone's seen it, discarding uncommitted changes, and undoing a commit that's already been shared.

learningObjectives.text: Match a real undo situation to the correct git command
Explain why undoing an already-shared commit needs a different approach than undoing a private one

contentSections.title: Three different "oops", three different fixes

contentSections.body: You commit, then immediately notice a typo in the commit message. Separately, another day, you've been editing a file for ten minutes, hate the direction, and just want it back exactly how it was at the last commit. A third day, you find a bug that was introduced three commits ago, in a commit your teammate already pulled onto their machine. All three are "undo" — but they're not the same problem.

contentSections.scenario: Three real situations, and the commands available: git commit --amend (rewrite your most recent commit), git restore <file> (discard uncommitted changes to a file, back to the last commit), git revert <commit> (add a brand new commit that undoes an earlier one, without erasing it from history).
contentSections.question: Which command fixes which situation? Select all three matches.

items.label: git commit --amend — for the typo in the message you just committed, before anyone's pulled it
git restore <file> — for throwing away ten minutes of uncommitted edits and going back to the last commit
git revert <commit> — for undoing a bug from three commits ago that a teammate already pulled
git commit --amend — for undoing the already-shared three-commits-ago bug

explanation.amend_typo: Correct match. --amend only rewrites your most recent commit, and only cleanly while it's still local — exactly the typo case.
explanation.restore_uncommitted: Correct match. Uncommitted changes to a file aren't in history at all yet, so restoring just throws the working-directory edits away and returns to the last real commit.
explanation.revert_shared: Correct match. A commit someone else already has is now shared history — revert adds a new commit that undoes it, which everyone can safely pull, instead of secretly rewriting something they've already built on top of.
explanation.amend_shared: This is the mismatch. --amend rewrites history — fine while a commit is still private and only on your machine, but if a teammate already pulled it, amending creates two different, conflicting versions of "the same" commit, and their copy and yours no longer agree. That's what revert exists to avoid.

contentSections.body: The dividing line across all three is whether the thing you're undoing has been shared with anyone else yet. `--amend` and `reset` both rewrite history — perfectly fine, even convenient, as long as the commit in question is still only on your machine. The moment a commit has been pushed and someone else might have it, rewriting it stops being a private cleanup and starts being a way to create two conflicting versions of the same commit that no longer agree with each other. `revert` sidesteps that entirely: instead of pretending the bad commit never happened, it adds a new commit that does the opposite of it — the history stays honest and everyone's copy stays in sync.
Not-yet-shared mistakes can be rewritten (`--amend`, `reset`). Already-shared ones get undone with a new commit on top (`revert`) — never rewritten out of existence.

contentSections.title: The command that can actually lose work

contentSections.body: You search "undo git commit" and find `git reset --hard HEAD~1`. It works — the bad commit is gone. It also silently discarded the uncommitted changes you had sitting in your working directory at the time, which weren't part of that commit at all and are now gone too.

contentSections.scenario: `git reset --hard` moves your project back to an earlier commit — and, in the same move, discards *all* uncommitted changes currently in your working directory, even ones that had nothing to do with the commit you're undoing.
contentSections.question: Someone runs `git reset --hard HEAD~1` to undo their last commit, expecting only that commit to disappear. They also lose an unrelated file they'd been editing for twenty minutes and never committed. What actually happened?

options.label: --hard discards uncommitted changes as part of resetting, regardless of whether they're related to the commit being undone
This is a git bug — reset should only touch the specific commit named
The twenty minutes of edits were never really lost, just hidden somewhere recoverable by default

feedback.hard_wipes: Right. --hard doesn't distinguish "changes from the commit I'm undoing" from "unrelated uncommitted work sitting in the working directory" — it wipes the working directory back to match the target commit exactly, discarding anything uncommitted along the way. This is real, permanent data loss if that work wasn't committed or saved anywhere else.
feedback.bug: This is git working exactly as designed, not a bug — --hard's entire job is to force the working directory to match a specific commit, discarding anything in between. It's dangerous specifically because it does exactly what it's supposed to do, silently.
feedback.hidden: Nothing rescues you here by default. --hard genuinely discards uncommitted changes; there's no automatic safety net unless you'd committed, stashed, or otherwise saved that work somewhere before running it.

contentSections.mechanism: `git reset --hard` is dangerous specifically because "hard" means it also overwrites your working directory to match the target commit — silently discarding any uncommitted changes in its path, related or not. The safer instinct as a beginner: commit or stash anything you care about before running any command with "hard" or "force" in it, and reach for `git revert` by default when you're not certain reset's exact blast radius.

contentSections.body: `reset --hard` doesn't just undo a commit — it wipes your working directory back to match it, taking any uncommitted work along with it. Commit or stash first, or reach for revert instead.

title: Branches, and working on something without breaking what works
description: A branch is a separate, safe line of work — try something risky without touching the version that already works, then merge it back in once it's actually ready.

learningObjectives.text: Create a branch and switch between it and main
Explain what a merge conflict is and read its markers

contentSections.title: A separate line of work you can throw away

contentSections.body: Your app works. You want to try restructuring how it saves data — a real change, not a tiny tweak, and you're not sure it'll actually work out. If you just start editing on top of the working version and it goes badly, you're stuck untangling a mess to get back to what worked.

contentSections.scenario: `main` is the branch holding your working project. `git branch new-storage` creates a new branch starting from main's current state — an exact copy of the history so far, but able to diverge from that point forward. `git checkout new-storage` (or `git switch new-storage`) moves you onto it, so your edits now happen there instead of on main.
contentSections.question: You make ten commits of restructuring work on `new-storage`, and it turns out to be a bad idea. What's true of `main` the whole time you were doing this?

options.label: main was never touched — it's exactly as it was before you started, ready to switch back to instantly
main automatically absorbed your changes as you committed them
main is now broken until you manually undo the ten commits on new-storage

feedback.untouched: Right. Commits made on new-storage only exist on new-storage. main sits completely untouched the entire time — switching back to it with `git checkout main` puts you right back at the exact working state you started from, and you can delete new-storage entirely with nothing lost from main.
feedback.absorbed: Branches don't sync automatically — that's the entire point of having them. Commits on new-storage stay on new-storage until you deliberately merge them into main. Nothing crosses over on its own.
feedback.broken: main was never edited, so there's nothing on it to undo. The ten commits live entirely on new-storage; abandoning that branch (or just never merging it) leaves main exactly as it always was.

contentSections.concept: A branch is an independent line of commits starting from a shared point. Work on one branch doesn't affect any other branch until you deliberately merge it — which is what makes branches a genuinely safe place to try something that might not work out: worst case, you abandon the branch and main was never at risk.

contentSections.body: The everyday flow: `git checkout -b new-storage` creates the branch and switches to it in one command. You commit normally while on it — exactly the same `git add` / `git commit` as before, just recorded onto this branch instead of main. `git checkout main` switches back at any point, showing you main exactly as it was. When the new work is actually ready, `git merge new-storage` (run while on main) brings those commits into main for good.
A branch lets you commit real work without touching the branch you started from — abandoning it costs nothing, because nothing was shared until you merged.

contentSections.title: When two branches changed the same lines

contentSections.body: You merge `new-storage` into `main`. Git stops and says there's a conflict in `data.js`. It turns out someone (maybe you, on main, in the meantime) changed the exact same line that new-storage also changed — git can't guess which version you actually want.

contentSections.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
function saveData(entry) {
  localStorage.setItem('log', JSON.stringify(entry));
}
=======
function saveData(entry) {
  return db.save('log', entry);
}
>>>>>>> new-storage
contentSections.question: This is what a merge conflict looks like inside the file after git stops. What do the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> markers actually mean?

options.label: Everything between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your current branch's version; everything between ======= and >>>>>>> new-storage is the other branch's version — you choose (or combine) and delete the markers
The code is now permanently broken and the file needs to be rewritten from scratch
Git already picked the correct version automatically — the markers are just a log of what it decided

feedback.correct: Right. Git found two different versions of the same lines and can't guess which one you want, so it inserts both, clearly labeled, and stops. Your job: decide what the final code should be — one version, the other, a hand-merged combination of both — then delete all three marker lines. Nothing is broken; git is asking a question it genuinely cannot answer on its own.
feedback.broken: Nothing is broken — the file just temporarily contains both candidate versions, clearly marked, until you resolve it. Once you pick/combine and delete the markers, it's a normal working file again.
feedback.auto: Git didn't decide anything here — that's exactly why it stopped and left both versions in the file for you to resolve by hand. If it could safely guess, it would have merged automatically without bothering you at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The two versions genuinely disagree about what saveData should do — one saves to localStorage, one saves to a database. There's no safe automatic answer, which is precisely when git asks a human. Resolving means picking the actual intended behavior (possibly neither original version alone), then committing the resolved file.

contentSections.body: A conflict means two branches changed the same lines differently — git shows you both versions clearly marked and waits for a human decision, rather than guessing wrong.

title: Putting it somewhere that isn't your laptop
description: A remote repository (like GitHub) is a second, off-device copy of your project's full history — push to send your commits there, pull to bring anyone else's back, and .gitignore to keep secrets and clutter out of it entirely.

learningObjectives.text: Push local commits to a remote repository and pull changes back down
Identify what belongs in .gitignore and why

contentSections.title: Local history is still only in one place

contentSections.body: Everything from this module so far — commits, undoing, branches — has all been happening in one folder on one laptop. If that laptop is stolen, dies, or gets a full disk failure tomorrow, all of it, the entire meticulously-messaged history, goes with it.

contentSections.question: You've been committing carefully for weeks — clean messages, sensible branches. Does having a good git history on your laptop protect that work if the laptop itself is lost or destroyed?
contentSections.hint: Git's history lives inside the project folder on whichever machine it's running on — ask where that folder physically is.
contentSections.answer: No, not by itself. Every commit you've made so far exists only inside the `.git` folder on that one laptop. A perfect commit history is still just one copy, in one place — exactly as vulnerable as any other file on that machine. Protecting it means putting a copy somewhere else entirely: a remote repository, most commonly on GitHub.

contentSections.body: `git remote add origin <url>` connects your local project to a remote repository you've created (on GitHub or similar) — a one-time setup step. From then on, `git push` sends your local commits up to it, and `git pull` brings down any commits that exist there but not locally yet — useful the moment you're working from more than one device, or with anyone else. `git clone <url>` is how you (or anyone else) gets a fresh, full copy of the project — history and all — onto a brand new machine.
A remote repository is a second copy of your entire history, off your device — push sends commits to it, pull brings others' back, clone gets a full working copy anywhere.

contentSections.title: What should never get pushed

contentSections.body: You push your project to a public GitHub repo, proud of it. Two days later you realize your API key — the one that bills your account — was sitting in a file that got committed and pushed in week one. It's now visible in the history, to anyone, forever, even if you delete it from the current file.

contentSections.scenario: A `.gitignore` file lists filenames and patterns git should never stage or commit, even with `git add .` — commonly things like `node_modules/` (huge, regeneratable), `.env` (secrets and API keys), and OS-generated clutter like `.DS_Store`.
contentSections.question: Why does deleting a secret from the current version of a file, after it was already committed and pushed weeks ago, not actually remove the danger?

options.label: The secret is still sitting in the old commits in the project's history — git doesn't forget past versions just because the current file changed
It does fully fix it — the current file is all that matters
GitHub automatically detects and removes secrets from all past commits

feedback.history_remembers: Right. Every commit is a permanent snapshot — deleting a secret in a new commit adds a new snapshot without it, but the old commit where it first appeared is still right there in the history, viewable, downloadable, and already possibly indexed by anyone who cloned or scraped it before you noticed. The real fix is rotating the leaked credential (making it invalid) — not just editing it out going forward.
feedback.fixed: The current file being clean doesn't erase the old commits — git's whole design is to keep every past snapshot, which is normally the point, but becomes the problem here. The secret is still recoverable from history.
feedback.auto_remove: GitHub doesn't do this automatically. Some tools scan for exposed secrets and warn you, which can prompt you to act — but nothing removes the old commit or invalidates the leaked key on its own.

contentSections.concept: A `.gitignore` file is a list of patterns git refuses to stage, checked before anything is added — it's the way you keep secrets, huge regeneratable folders, and OS clutter out of the history in the first place, which is far cheaper than trying to remove something after it's already been committed and pushed.

contentSections.body: Once a secret is committed and pushed, deleting it from the current file isn't enough — it's still in history. .gitignore exists to keep it out from the start.

title: Practice — Recover From Eight Version-Control Situations
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a real git situation, choose (or produce) the correct recovery.

learningObjectives.text: Choose the correct git command for a described real-world situation

contentSections.title: Eight situations, the commands from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: staging vs committing, the three undo situations, branching, merge conflicts, or what belongs in a remote versus what belongs in .gitignore.
Almost every real git situation is one of these eight, wearing slightly different clothes — situation first, then the command that fits it.

title: Lab — Put Your Project Under Version Control Properly
description: Take a real project of yours (or start a small new one) and put it under git properly, from a clean first commit through a branch-and-merge, to a working, pushed remote — building the habit this whole module has been aiming at.

learningObjectives.text: Initialize a git repository and build a real, meaningfully-messaged commit history
Create a branch, make a real change on it, and merge it back
Connect a local repository to a remote and push a working copy to it

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Everything in this module has been building toward this: a real project, under real version control, with a history that actually explains itself, at least one genuine branch-and-merge, and a working copy pushed somewhere that isn't your laptop.

contentSections.title: Put your project under version control properly
contentSections.brief: Pick a real project — something you've already built in this track, or a small new one if you'd rather. By the end of this lab it will have a clean git history with meaningful commits, at least one branch that was merged back in, a working .gitignore, and a working remote on GitHub you (or anyone else) could clone from scratch.
contentSections.deliverable: A repository with meaningful commit history and a working remote.

stages.title: Initialize and make a clean first commit
stages.instructions: Run `git init` in your project folder. Before your first commit, create a `.gitignore` that excludes at minimum `node_modules/` (if present) and any file holding a real secret or API key. Then stage and make your first commit with a message describing the project's starting state honestly (not "initial commit" alone — say what's actually there).
stages.checkpoint: `git status` shows a clean working directory, `git log` shows one real commit, and .gitignore correctly excludes anything that shouldn't be tracked.

stages.title: Build a real commit history
stages.instructions: Make at least three more commits, each one a genuinely separate, logical change (not one giant commit dumping everything at once), each with a message that names what changed and why — the same standard from lesson 2.
stages.checkpoint: `git log` shows at least four commits total, each with a specific, honest message a stranger could understand without opening the diff.

stages.title: Branch, change, merge
stages.instructions: Create a new branch for one real, contained change (a genuine improvement, not a throwaway). Commit it on that branch. Switch back to main and confirm the change isn't there. Then merge the branch into main and confirm it now is.
stages.checkpoint: You can show the change was absent from main before the merge and present after it — a real, demonstrated branch-and-merge, not just the commands run blind.

stages.title: Push to a real remote
stages.instructions: Create a repository on GitHub, connect it with `git remote add origin <url>`, and push your full history with `git push -u origin main`. Confirm on GitHub's website that your commit history — messages included — is really there.
stages.checkpoint: Your commit history is visible on GitHub, with the same messages you wrote locally, and no secrets appear anywhere in it.

rubric.criterion: History is real and honest
rubric.meets: At least four commits, each a genuinely separate logical change with a message naming what and why — not one giant commit or a string of "updates".

rubric.criterion: .gitignore actually protects what it should
rubric.meets: node_modules (if present) and any real secret/API key file are excluded before the first commit, not cleaned up after.

rubric.criterion: A branch was genuinely used, not just created
rubric.meets: A real change was committed on a separate branch, confirmed absent from main beforehand, then merged in and confirmed present.

rubric.criterion: The remote is real and complete
rubric.meets: The full commit history, with original messages, is visible on GitHub — not just a single squashed snapshot.

rubric.criterion: No secrets anywhere in the pushed history
rubric.meets: Checked deliberately, not assumed — including in commits made before the .gitignore existed, if any.

contentSections.body: A repository with a real, honest history and a working remote is the actual deliverable of this module — everything else was practice for building it.
