questions.explanation: Git never acts on its own — saving a file changes what's on disk, but a snapshot only gets recorded when you deliberately run `git add` and `git commit`.

questions.from: This module — Version Control
questions.prompt: You already pushed a commit and a teammate pulled it. You now realize it has a bug. Why is `git commit --amend` the wrong tool here, where `git revert` is right?

options.label: --amend rewrites a commit that's already shared, which can put your history and your teammate's out of sync; revert adds a new corrective commit that everyone can safely pull
--amend is slower to type than revert
There's no real difference — either works fine

questions.explanation: Rewriting a commit that someone else already has creates two disagreeing versions of "the same" commit. Revert avoids that by adding new history instead of rewriting old history.

questions.from: This module — Version Control
questions.prompt: What specifically makes `git reset --hard` risky compared to other undo commands?

options.label: It also discards uncommitted changes in your working directory, related or not, with no automatic recovery
It's risky only because it's rarely used, not because of what it does
It only affects the commit message, nothing else

questions.explanation: "Hard" means the working directory is forced to match the target commit exactly — any uncommitted work in the way is silently discarded, whether or not it was related to what you meant to undo.

questions.from: This module — Version Control
questions.prompt: You deleted a leaked API key from your file and committed that deletion. Is the key now safe?

options.label: Yes — the current version of the file is all that matters
No — the key is still visible in the earlier commit where it was first added; it needs to be rotated (invalidated), not just deleted going forward
Yes, as long as the repository is private

questions.explanation: Every commit is a permanent snapshot. The old commit containing the key still exists in history and is still recoverable, regardless of what later commits do — the actual fix is invalidating the leaked credential.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: From Getting Data From Elsewhere: what does fetch(url) actually return right away — the real data, or something else?

options.label: A Promise — the real data isn't ready yet, and await is what actually pauses for it
The real, final data, already parsed
Nothing — fetch only works inside a try/catch block

questions.explanation: fetch() returns a Promise immediately; the response isn't ready until later, which is exactly what `await` (inside an `async` function) waits for.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: From Getting Data From Elsewhere: a fetch request completes, but the server responds with a 404. Does try/catch alone catch this as an error?

options.label: No — a completed request with an error status doesn't throw; you need to separately check response.ok
Yes — any non-200 response automatically throws inside the try block
try/catch is irrelevant to fetch entirely

questions.explanation: try/catch handles requests that never complete (network failure). A request that completes but reports an error status doesn't throw on its own — checking response.ok is a separate, necessary step.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: From Getting Data From Elsewhere: why can't a secret API key be safely hidden inside frontend JavaScript, no matter how it's obscured?

options.label: Everything sent to the browser is fully downloaded and readable by anyone who opens dev tools — there's no genuine hiding place on the client
It can be hidden safely if the variable name is unclear
Browsers automatically encrypt all JavaScript before running it

questions.explanation: Frontend code is fully delivered to and readable in the browser — obscuring a key doesn't hide it, it just makes it slightly more annoying to find. A real secret has to live on a server the browser never sees directly.

questions.from: Previous module — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: From Getting Data From Elsewhere: what is an endpoint?

options.label: One specific URL that answers one specific question — the wrong endpoint returns real, valid data, just not the data you meant to ask for
Any URL on the internet that returns JSON
The final step of an async function

questions.explanation: An endpoint is a specific, published URL for a specific question. Calling the wrong one doesn't error — it just answers a different question than the one you intended.

questions.from: Three modules back — JavaScript in the Page
questions.prompt: From JavaScript in the Page: what's the risk of using textContent vs innerHTML to insert something a user typed?

options.label: innerHTML parses its input as real HTML, which is risky for user-typed content; textContent always inserts plain text safely
They're interchangeable with no difference
textContent is the risky one because it's newer

questions.explanation: textContent treats its input as plain text, always. innerHTML parses it as HTML — fine for your own trusted markup, dangerous for anything a user typed, since it could contain real (and malicious) tags.

questions.from: Four modules back — HTML: Structure and Meaning
questions.prompt: From HTML: Structure and Meaning: why does a page built entirely from <div class="nav"> instead of <nav> lose something, even styled identically?

options.label: Class names carry zero meaning to a screen reader — only the tag name itself is announced as structural information
div renders more slowly than nav
Nothing is lost — class names are equivalent to semantic tags

questions.explanation: Class names exist for CSS/JS to target — a screen reader announces the tag itself, not its class. Only a real semantic tag like <nav> communicates that structural role.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Testing by hand, and why it stops scaling
description: Clicking through your app to check a feature works is real testing — it just doesn't scale, because you can't feasibly re-check everything by hand after every change, and the thing that breaks is never the thing you were looking at.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why manual re-checking becomes impractical as a project grows
Define a regression as something that used to work breaking due to an unrelated change

contentSections.title: You can't remember to re-check everything

contentSections.body: You build a discount calculator for your shop project. You test it by hand: enter a price, check the discounted number looks right. It does. Two weeks later you add a coupon-code feature, touching a completely different part of the file. You don't think to re-check the discount calculator — why would you, you didn't touch it — and ship it. A customer's order comes out wrong. The discount calculator broke, silently, because the coupon code change edited a shared variable it also depended on.

contentSections.scenario: Four features in a small project, each hand-tested and working the day it was built: login, discount calculator, coupon codes, order total. Three weeks and several unrelated changes later, one of them is quietly broken.
contentSections.question: What's the actual reason manual testing misses this, even for a careful developer?

options.label: Manual testing only checks what you think to check, right now — it says nothing about features you built weeks ago that a later change might have silently affected
Manual testers are naturally careless people
The bug is unfindable by any method until a customer reports it

feedback.scope: Right. Manual testing checks exactly what's in front of you, right now — it has no memory of the other three features and no way to notice that changing shared code silently affected one of them, unless you happen to think to re-click through all of them, every single time, which nobody actually does at real project sizes.
feedback.careless: This isn't about carelessness — even a meticulous developer can't feasibly re-click through every feature by hand after every single change. The problem is structural, not a personal failing.
feedback.unfindable: It's very findable — an automated test for the discount calculator, run automatically after the coupon-code change, would have caught this the moment it broke, days before a customer ever saw it. The problem is that manual testing doesn't run automatically or remember to check.

contentSections.concept: A regression is exactly this: a feature that used to work breaking because of a change somewhere else, unrelated on the surface. Manual testing only verifies what you deliberately check, at the moment you check it — it has no way to protect features you built earlier from being silently broken by later changes, because nobody re-tests everything by hand after every edit.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument that manual testing is wrong — clicking through a new feature to see if it works is a completely normal, necessary first check. The problem is specifically what it *can't* do: it doesn't run itself, it doesn't remember what needs re-checking, and it doesn't scale past a handful of features before re-checking everything by hand after every change becomes a full-time job nobody actually does. Automated tests are code that does the re-checking for you — the same check, saved once, and re-run automatically as many times as you want, in seconds, for free.
Manual testing checks what you think to check, right now. It can't protect old features from being silently broken by a change somewhere else — that's what a regression is.

contentSections.title: The check that runs itself

contentSections.body: Imagine you'd written down, the day you built the discount calculator, exactly what "correct" meant: price 100 with a 10% discount should equal 90. Now imagine that check ran itself, automatically, every time you changed anything in the project — not just when you happened to remember.

contentSections.question: If an automated test for the discount calculator existed and ran automatically after the coupon-code change, would it have caught the bug before a customer did?
contentSections.hint: The test doesn't know or care what else changed — it just re-checks the exact thing it was written to check, every time.
contentSections.answer: Yes — that's the entire point of an automated test. It doesn't need you to remember it exists or to think "maybe I should re-check the discount calculator." It's code that runs the same check every time, and if the coupon-code change broke the shared variable the discount calculator depended on, the test would fail immediately — while you're still looking at the coupon-code change, not three weeks later from a customer complaint.

contentSections.body: This is the actual shift this module is teaching: turning a manual check you did once into a small piece of code that does the same check, permanently, automatically, for free, forever. It's not a replacement for understanding your own code — it's a way of never having to trust your memory about which features still work after you've changed something else.
An automated test is a manual check you did once, saved as code, so it re-runs itself instead of depending on you remembering to redo it.

title: Your first automated test
description: A test calls your function with a known input and checks the output against what you expect — written once as code, using a small testing library, and re-run any time.

learningObjectives.text: Write a test that calls a function and asserts its return value
Explain the three parts every test needs: input, the call, and the expected result

contentSections.title: Input, call, expected result

contentSections.body: You have a real function: `applyDiscount(price, percent)`, which should return the discounted price. Testing it by hand means typing numbers into the browser console and eyeballing the result. Testing it automatically means writing that exact same check, once, as code.

contentSections.problem: Write an automated test confirming applyDiscount(100, 10) returns 90 — using vitest, a small testing library that runs in the terminal.

steps.label: Import the tools and the function
steps.work:
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { applyDiscount } from './discount.js';
steps.why: test defines one check; expect makes an assertion about a value. Both come from the testing library, imported like any other code.

steps.label: Describe the check in plain words
steps.work: test('applies a 10% discount correctly', () => { ... });
steps.why: The string is the test's name — shown in the output, pass or fail. Write it as a sentence describing what should be true, not just a label.

steps.label: Call the real function with a known input
steps.work: const result = applyDiscount(100, 10);
steps.why: This is the exact same call you'd make by hand in the console — just saved as code instead of typed and thrown away.

steps.label: Assert the result matches what you expect
steps.work: expect(result).toBe(90);
steps.why: toBe checks for an exact match. If applyDiscount ever returns anything other than 90 for this input — today, or after some future change — this line is what catches it.

faded.problem: Write a test confirming celsiusToFahrenheit(0) returns 32.

blanks.prompt: Import test and expect from the testing library
blanks.why: Same import every time — these are the two building blocks every test needs.

blanks.prompt: Call the function with the known input and store the result
blanks.why: Exactly the call you'd make by hand — 0°C should convert to 32°F.
toBe(32) fails loudly if the function ever stops returning 32 for this input.

contentSections.procedure: Import test and expect, call the real function with a known input, then assert the result with expect(...).toBe(...) — the same shape for almost every simple test.

contentSections.body: A test is three things: a known input, the real function call, and an assertion about what the result should be.

contentSections.title: Running it and reading the result

contentSections.body: You've written the test. It's sitting in a file. Nothing happens until you actually run it — and the whole reason it's worth writing is what happens the next time something breaks.

contentSections.scenario: Running `npm test` (or your project's equivalent) executes every test file in the project and prints a result for each: a green checkmark and "1 passed" if the assertion held, or a red failure showing exactly what was expected versus what was actually returned.
contentSections.question: You change applyDiscount's rounding logic for an unrelated reason, and its test now fails, showing "expected 90, received 89.99999". What does this failure actually tell you?

options.label: Something about your change affected this function's output — worth investigating before you ship, even though you didn't mean to touch it
The test itself is broken and should be deleted
89.99999 is close enough, so the failure can be ignored

feedback.caught: Exactly right — this is the test doing its job. You didn't have to remember to re-check applyDiscount by hand; the test noticed on its own, the moment it stopped matching what you'd declared correct. Whether the fix is in your rounding logic or the test's expected value needs updating is a real judgment call — but you get to make that call deliberately, instead of finding out from a customer.
feedback.delete: Deleting a failing test doesn't fix anything — it just removes the thing that was telling you something changed. The failure is information; ignoring the messenger doesn't un-happen the actual behavior change.
feedback.ignore: A close-but-not-exact result for money specifically (89.99999 instead of 90) is exactly the kind of thing worth catching — floating-point rounding errors in prices are a real, common bug. "Close enough" for currency is often not actually close enough.

contentSections.concept: A test failure isn't a punishment — it's the exact information you'd otherwise have to discover by accident weeks later. Every failure is a specific, honest report: here's what was expected, here's what actually happened, you decide what to do about it.

contentSections.body: Running tests turns "I hope I didn't break anything" into an actual answer, printed in seconds, every time.

title: Testing the edges rather than the middle
description: The input most likely to reveal a bug is rarely the comfortable, obvious one — empty input, zero, negative numbers, and exact boundaries are where real bugs actually live.

learningObjectives.text: Identify edge cases a function needs testing against beyond the obvious happy path
Write a test for a boundary condition (an exact threshold value)

contentSections.title: The happy path is the least useful test

contentSections.body: You write `applyDiscount(100, 10)` returns 90 as your one test, it passes, and you move on. In production, someone applies a 100% discount code and the price goes negative. Someone else enters a discount of -10 (a typo) and the price goes *up*. Your one test never had a chance to catch either, because it only ever tried the easy, expected case.

contentSections.scenario: Test cases for applyDiscount(price, percent), sorted into two piles: the "happy path" (typical, expected input) and "edges" (unusual but real values a function actually has to handle).
contentSections.question: Which of these is the happy-path case, least likely to reveal a real bug?

options.label: applyDiscount(100, 10) — a normal price with a normal discount
applyDiscount(100, 100) — a 100% discount, where the result should be exactly 0, not negative
applyDiscount(100, -10) — a negative discount, which shouldn't be allowed to raise the price

feedback.happy: Right. This is the case a function is most obviously built for, and the one most likely to already work by the time you're testing — it's worth having as a test, but it's the least likely one to actually catch a bug, precisely because it's the case every implementation naturally handles correctly first.
feedback.edge1: This is one of the edges, not the happy path — a 100% discount is a real, valid input that a naive implementation might mishandle (returning something other than a clean 0, or breaking on the boundary).
feedback.edge2: This is the other edge here — a negative percentage shouldn't be accepted as a valid discount at all, and testing it is what catches a function that doesn't validate its input.

contentSections.concept: The happy path — typical, well-behaved input — is worth one test, but it's the input every implementation is naturally built and checked against first, so it's the least likely place a real bug survives. Edge cases — zero, negative numbers, empty input, the maximum allowed value, one past it — are where implementations quietly disagree about what "correct" even means, which is exactly where bugs hide.

contentSections.body: A short, genuinely useful checklist for almost any function: what happens with zero? With a negative number, if negative doesn't make sense for this input? With an empty string or empty list? With the single largest or smallest value the function is meant to handle? None of these are exotic — they're all real values a real user (or a typo, or another part of your own code) will eventually pass in. A function that's only ever been tested against comfortable, expected input hasn't really been tested against the inputs most likely to break it.
The happy path confirms a function works when everything's normal. Edge cases are what actually reveal whether it's correct.

contentSections.title: The exact line where behavior changes

contentSections.body: A senior-discount function gives 15% off if age is 65 or older. You test age 70 (works) and age 30 (correctly gets no discount). You never test age 65 itself — the exact boundary — and it turns out the code was written with `age > 65` instead of `age >= 65`, silently excluding every 65-year-old.

contentSections.scenario: A function is written as `if (age > 65) return 0.15; else return 0;` — intended to match the rule "65 or older gets 15% off."
contentSections.question: For exactly age 65, what discount does this code actually return, in percent (not the intended answer — the real one, as written)?
contentSections.explanation: `age > 65` is strictly greater than — age 65 itself fails that check and falls through to the else, returning 0. The intended rule was "65 or older," which needed `age >= 65`. This is a classic boundary bug, and it's specifically invisible to tests at age 70 and age 30 — both give the same result whether the code says > or >=. Only testing the exact boundary value (65) catches the difference.

contentSections.body: Boundary bugs (> vs >=) are invisible to tests on either side of the line — only a test at the exact boundary value catches them.

title: A test that would fail if the code were wrong
description: A test that passes no matter what the code does isn't testing anything — the only way to know a test is real is to check it can actually fail.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a test that would pass regardless of whether the code is correct
Explain how deliberately breaking the code verifies a test is genuinely checking something

contentSections.title: A test that can't fail is decoration

contentSections.body: A teammate proudly shows you their test suite: 40 tests, all green. You look at one: `expect(applyDiscount(100, 10)).toBeDefined();` — it only checks that *something* came back, not that the something is 90. Change the function to always return the string "banana" instead of a number, and this test still passes.

contentSections.question: What's actually wrong with this test, given that it does pass right now?

options.label: toBeDefined() only checks that a value exists at all — it would pass even if applyDiscount returned the wrong number, or a completely wrong type
Nothing is wrong — a passing test is a passing test
The import statement is wrong

feedback.weak: Right. toBeDefined() only confirms the function returned *something* rather than undefined — it says nothing about whether that something is correct. A completely broken applyDiscount that always returns 0, or -5, or the string "oops", would pass this test just as easily as a correct one. The test provides false confidence: green, but meaningless.
feedback.fine: A test passing doesn't mean it's checking anything real — that's exactly the trap here. This test would pass for almost any output at all, correct or not, which makes "it's passing" worthless as a signal.
feedback.import: The import is fine — applyDiscount is genuinely imported and called. The problem is entirely in what the assertion actually checks, which is far weaker than it looks.

contentSections.flawExplanation: toBeDefined() checks existence, not correctness. The fix is a specific assertion — expect(result).toBe(90) — that only passes for the one actual correct value, and genuinely fails if applyDiscount ever returns anything else.

contentSections.body: This is worth taking seriously: a green test suite feels like safety, but a suite full of weak assertions like toBeDefined(), or tests that never actually call the function being tested, or tests that assert something trivially true, gives you the *feeling* of safety with none of the actual protection. The number of tests you have matters far less than whether each one would genuinely fail if the code were wrong.
A test that passes for almost any output isn't testing anything — it's confidence theater. Check what it actually asserts, not just whether it's green.

contentSections.title: The proof: break it on purpose

contentSections.body: How do you actually know a specific test is meaningful, rather than just trusting that it looks reasonable? There's a concrete way to check, and it's the exact standard this module's lab holds every test to.

contentSections.question: You have a test: expect(applyDiscount(100, 10)).toBe(90). To prove this test would genuinely catch a real bug, what's the most direct thing to do?
contentSections.hint: The test's whole job is to fail when the code is wrong — so check that it actually does, on purpose, once.
contentSections.answer: Temporarily break the real implementation on purpose — for example, change the discount math to subtract the wrong amount — and re-run the test. If it goes red, the test is proven to genuinely check something real; if it still passes on clearly broken code, the test (not the code) has a problem and needs fixing. Then revert the deliberate break, confirm the test passes again on the real, correct code, and you're done. This one deliberate break-and-revert is the actual proof a test is meaningful, not just green.

contentSections.body: This isn't paranoia — it's the cheapest possible check on your own test suite, and it catches a genuinely common beginner mistake: writing a test, seeing it pass, and assuming that means the test is good, when really it might pass no matter what the code does. Breaking the implementation on purpose, confirming red, then reverting, takes under a minute per test and is the difference between a suite that actually protects you and one that only looks like it does.
Seeing a test pass proves nothing on its own. Seeing it fail against deliberately broken code is what proves it's actually testing something.

title: Running tests without thinking about it
description: A test suite only protects you if you actually run it — one command that runs every test, a watch mode that reruns automatically, and reading a failure message instead of skipping past it.

learningObjectives.text: Run a project's full test suite with a single command
Read a failure message to identify what changed and where to look

contentSections.title: One command, every test

contentSections.body: You have twelve tests spread across four files. Running each one individually, remembering which file covers what, is its own kind of manual chore — exactly the thing this whole module is supposed to remove.

contentSections.scenario: `npm test` (configured once, in package.json, to point at your testing library) runs every test file in the project in one go, printing a single summary: how many passed, how many failed, and which ones.
contentSections.question: Why does having one single command matter, beyond just being slightly faster to type?

options.label: It removes the last excuse not to run the tests — one command, no decisions about which files matter, makes running them a genuine habit instead of a chore
It doesn't matter much — running each test file separately gives the exact same information
It's required because tests can't be run individually

feedback.habit: Right. The value isn't really about speed — it's that a single, memorable command with zero setup removes every reason to skip running your tests. "I'll just run the ones I think are relevant" is exactly the same reasoning that let the discount calculator bug from lesson 1 slip through — one command that runs everything removes that judgment call entirely.
feedback.same: Technically the same tests run either way — but in practice, remembering which files to run, and doing that every time, is real friction, and friction is what makes people skip testing before a change "that shouldn't affect anything."
feedback.required: Tests can usually be run individually too (most testing libraries support this) — the point of a single all-tests command isn't that it's the only option, it's that it's the easiest one, which is what actually gets used consistently.

contentSections.concept: A single command that runs your entire suite turns "should I test this?" into a non-decision — you just run it, every time, the same way, with nothing to remember or judge. That's what actually makes testing a habit instead of a task people quietly skip under time pressure.

contentSections.body: One command for the whole suite removes every excuse to skip running it — that's the actual value, more than the time saved.

contentSections.title: Reading a failure instead of skipping past it

contentSections.body: A test fails: `expected 90, received 100`. It's tempting to glance at red text, sigh, and either guess-fix something or comment the test out to make it go away. Neither actually tells you what happened.

contentSections.scenario: A failure message reads: "applies a 10% discount correctly — expected 90, received 100." The test name, the expected value, and the actual value are all shown.
contentSections.question: Received 100 instead of 90 for a 10% discount — what does this specific failure tell you about where to look?

options.label: The discount isn't being applied at all — the function returned the original price unchanged, so the actual math (or the call to it) is likely broken or missing
Nothing useful — a failure just means something is broken, generically
The test itself must be wrong, since 100 is a valid number

feedback.not_applied: Right. "Received 100" (the original price, unchanged) instead of 90 is a specific clue: the discount calculation isn't happening at all, not that it's slightly off. That narrows the search immediately — check whether the discount math is even being applied, before checking anything about rounding or edge cases.
feedback.nothing: The message is specific and useful: expected vs. received tells you exactly how far off, and often in what direction, the actual behavior is from what you declared correct. Treating every failure as generically "something's broken" throws away real information.
feedback.test_wrong: 100 being a valid number doesn't mean the test is wrong — the test's whole claim is that applyDiscount(100, 10) should specifically be 90, and getting the unchanged original price back is a strong signal the discount logic itself isn't running.

contentSections.mechanism: A well-written failure message is diagnostic information, not just a red flag — expected vs. actual tells you the direction and shape of what's wrong (unchanged output usually means a step is missing entirely; a slightly-off number usually means the calculation itself has a bug). Reading it before touching any code saves real time over guessing.

contentSections.body: A failure message's expected-vs-actual gap is a real clue, not just a red light — read it before you start guessing at a fix.

title: Practice — Write Tests for Eight Functions
description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a function, write or choose the test that actually checks it correctly.

learningObjectives.text: Write or evaluate a test's assertion against a described function

contentSections.title: Eight functions, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these comes back to something from this module: input/call/assert, testing edges instead of just the happy path, boundary values, and a test that would actually fail if the code were wrong.
The same handful of questions, every time: what's the input, what's the real expected output, and would this test actually fail if the code were broken?

title: Lab — Add a Test Suite to Your Project
description: Take a real project of yours and give it a genuine test suite — happy-path and edge-case tests for its real functions, with every single one proven capable of failing by deliberately breaking the code it tests.

learningObjectives.text: Set up a testing library and write a real, running test suite for an existing project
Write tests covering both the happy path and genuine edge cases
Prove each test is meaningful by showing it fails against a deliberately broken version

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real project with at least two or three functions that take input and return a value — the discount calculator, a form validator, anything from earlier in this track. By the end of this lab it has a real test suite, and you'll have proven, not assumed, that every test actually works.

contentSections.title: Add a test suite to your project
contentSections.brief: Choose two or three functions from a real project of yours that take input and return a value. Set up a testing library, write tests for each — happy path and genuine edge cases — and prove every single test can actually fail before calling it done.
contentSections.deliverable: A suite where every test has been shown to fail against a broken version.

stages.title: Set up the test runner
stages.instructions: Install a testing library (vitest is a reasonable default) and confirm you can run one trivial test (like expect(1 + 1).toBe(2)) with your project's test command before writing anything real.
stages.checkpoint: Running your test command shows one passing test, proving the setup itself works before you build on it.

stages.title: Happy-path tests for two or three real functions
stages.instructions: For each chosen function, write at least one test using a normal, expected input and the exact correct output — not toBeDefined() or anything that would pass regardless of what the function returns.
stages.checkpoint: Every happy-path test asserts a specific expected value with toBe (or similar), and all of them currently pass against your real code.

stages.title: Edge-case tests
stages.instructions: For each function, add at least one edge-case test — zero, a negative number where it shouldn't be allowed, an empty input, or an exact boundary value, whichever genuinely applies to that function. If a test reveals a real bug in your existing code, note it — you don't have to fix it in this lab, but you do have to write down what you found.
stages.checkpoint: Each function has at least one edge-case test beyond the happy path, and you have a written note of anything a test actually caught.

stages.title: Prove every test can fail
stages.instructions: For each test, temporarily break the real function it tests (change a number, flip a comparison, remove a step) and re-run the suite to confirm that specific test goes red. Then revert the break and confirm it passes again. Do this for every test, not just one — a test you didn't personally watch fail is a test you're only assuming is real.
stages.checkpoint: You can state, for every single test in the suite, that you personally watched it fail on broken code and pass again on the real code.

rubric.criterion: The suite actually runs
rubric.meets: A single command runs every test and prints a clear pass/fail summary.

rubric.criterion: Assertions are specific, not decorative
rubric.meets: Every test asserts an exact expected value — no toBeDefined() or similar assertions that would pass regardless of correctness.

rubric.criterion: Both happy-path and real edge cases are covered
rubric.meets: Each tested function has at least one normal-input test and at least one genuine edge case (zero, negative, empty, or boundary, as applicable).

rubric.criterion: Every test is proven, not assumed, to work
rubric.meets: Each test has been individually watched failing against a deliberately broken version of the code, then passing again once reverted.

rubric.criterion: Any bug a test caught is written down
rubric.meets: If an edge-case test revealed a real existing bug, it's noted explicitly, even if not fixed in this lab.

contentSections.body: A test suite you've watched fail on purpose, function by function, is a test suite you can actually trust — one you've only ever seen pass is still an assumption.

title: Checkpoint — Checking Your Own Work
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Version Control, two reaching back into Remembering Things and JavaScript in the Page. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Checking Your Own Work

questions.from: This module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: Why does manual testing fail to protect a feature you built weeks ago from a change made somewhere else today?

options.label: Manual testing only checks what you deliberately re-check, right now — it has no memory of old features a later change might silently affect
Manual testing is simply less accurate than automated testing at the moment it's performed
It doesn't fail — manual testing catches every regression as long as you're careful

questions.explanation: Manual testing has no memory and doesn't run itself — it only verifies whatever you happen to click through at that moment, leaving unrelated older features unprotected from silent regressions.

questions.from: This module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: What three things does a basic automated test need?

options.label: A known input, a real call to the function, and an assertion about the expected result
A description, a screenshot, and a manual sign-off
Just an assertion — the input and call are optional

questions.explanation: A test calls the real function with a known input, then asserts what the result should be — all three parts are needed for the test to mean anything.

questions.from: This module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: A test uses `expect(result).toBeDefined()` instead of checking the actual value. What's the real problem with this?

options.label: It would pass even if the function returned a completely wrong value — it only checks something came back, not that it's correct
toBeDefined() is invalid syntax and would cause a crash
Nothing — a passing test is proof the code is correct

questions.explanation: toBeDefined() only confirms a value exists, not that it's the right one — a badly broken function could still pass this check, giving false confidence.

questions.from: This module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: What's the concrete way to prove a specific test is actually meaningful, not just green?

options.label: Temporarily break the real code it tests and confirm the test fails, then revert and confirm it passes again
Run the test a second time — if it passes twice, it's proven
Check that the test file is long enough

questions.explanation: Deliberately breaking the implementation and watching the test go red is the only real proof it checks something genuine — a test that never fails on broken code isn't actually testing anything.

questions.from: Previous module — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: why is `git commit --amend` the wrong tool for fixing a commit a teammate already pulled?

options.label: It rewrites shared history, which can put your copy and theirs out of sync — revert adds a new commit instead
It's not wrong — amend works fine on shared commits too
Amend only works on the very first commit in a project

questions.explanation: Rewriting a commit someone else already has creates two disagreeing versions of "the same" commit — revert avoids this by adding new history instead.

questions.from: Previous module — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: what does `git reset --hard` do to uncommitted changes in your working directory?

options.label: Discards them, related or not, with no automatic backup
Leaves them completely untouched
Automatically commits them first for safety

questions.explanation: "Hard" forces the working directory to match the target commit, silently discarding any uncommitted work in its path.

questions.from: Previous module — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: why does deleting a leaked API key from the current file and committing that deletion not fully fix the leak?

options.label: The key is still visible in the earlier commit that first added it — it needs to be rotated, not just edited out going forward
It does fully fix it — only the current file matters
Deleting a secret from a file is impossible once committed

questions.explanation: Every commit is a permanent snapshot — the earlier commit with the key is still in history and recoverable, regardless of later changes.

questions.from: Previous module — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: what does a merge conflict mean?

options.label: Two branches changed the same lines differently, and git can't safely guess which version you want
One of the two branches has a syntax error
The remote repository is unreachable

questions.explanation: Git stops and shows both versions, clearly marked, only when it genuinely can't tell which change should win — a human has to decide.

questions.from: Three modules back — Remembering Things
questions.prompt: From Remembering Things: why does JSON.parse throwing a real error on corrupted saved data actually matter, compared to most type mismatches in this track?

options.label: It fails loudly instead of quietly, which is what makes wrapping it in try/catch possible — most type mismatches fail silently instead
It doesn't matter — JSON.parse never fails on bad data
It only affects browser storage, never real user data

questions.explanation: JSON.parse throwing a real, catchable error on invalid JSON is what makes try/catch meaningful around it — turning a corrupted save into a deliberate recovery instead of a silent wrong value or a crash.

questions.from: Four modules back — JavaScript in the Page
questions.prompt: From JavaScript in the Page: what does an input field's .value type as, even for a field meant to hold a number?

options.label: A string, always — it needs Number(...) before real arithmetic
A number, automatically, if type="number" is set on the input
Whatever type the surrounding code declares

questions.explanation: Every input's .value is a string regardless of the input's type attribute — converting it explicitly with Number(...) is a required step before doing math on it.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: When one file stops being enough
description: One file is the right amount of structure for a small script — the moment you're scrolling to find things, or two people's changes keep colliding on the same lines, it's a sign the project has outgrown it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify concrete symptoms that a single-file project has outgrown that structure
Explain why splitting files too early has its own real cost

contentSections.title: One file is fine, until it isn't

contentSections.body: Your project started as a single `app.js` — reasonable, since it was one form and one calculation. Eight weeks and a dozen features later, it's 900 lines. You need to fix a bug in the discount logic, and finding it means scrolling past the login code, the API calls, and three other features first, none of which have anything to do with the bug.

contentSections.scenario: Four real projects at different sizes: (1) a 40-line script that converts temperatures, (2) a 900-line app.js mixing login, discount logic, API calls and form handling, (3) a well-organized project already split into login.js, discount.js, api.js, forms.js, (4) a brand-new two-day-old project with one small feature.
contentSections.question: Which of these is actually a sign the project has outgrown a single file, not just a matter of taste?

options.label: The 900-line app.js mixing several unrelated features — finding anything requires scrolling past code that has nothing to do with what you're changing
The 40-line temperature converter — it should be split into multiple files for good practice
The brand-new two-day-old single-feature project

feedback.app900: Right. The concrete symptom is real: you can't find or change one feature without wading through unrelated code for several others. That's not a style preference — it's friction that gets worse every week the project grows, and splitting related code into its own file directly removes it.
feedback.convert: A 40-line script doing one job is exactly the case where one file is still the right amount of structure — splitting it into multiple files would add navigation overhead (which file was that in again?) with nothing to show for it.
feedback.new: A brand-new project with one small feature hasn't hit any of the real symptoms yet — splitting preemptively, before there's an actual reason, tends to create empty-feeling files and premature decisions about a structure that hasn't been earned yet.

contentSections.concept: The real signal that a project has outgrown a single file isn't size in the abstract — it's a concrete cost you can point to: scrolling past unrelated code to find what you need, two unrelated features' code physically tangled together, or (once you're working with anyone else) two people's changes landing on the same lines because everything lives in one place. Splitting before any of that is true is optimizing for a problem you don't have yet.

contentSections.body: This cuts both ways, which is the part beginners often miss: splitting a 40-line project into five files doesn't make it better-organized, it makes it *harder* to follow, because now understanding one small feature means opening several files instead of scrolling a few screens in one. Structure is supposed to reduce the cost of finding and changing things — if a split adds more searching than it removes, it's not helping yet, no matter how professional it looks.
The reason to split a file is a concrete cost you can point to — scrolling past unrelated code, tangled features, colliding changes — not size alone or how it looks.

contentSections.title: Splitting too early has a cost too

contentSections.body: You've just started a new project — one page, one feature. You've heard "organize your code properly" enough times that you create `utils/`, `components/`, `helpers/`, `services/` before writing a single real line. Two days in, you have twelve nearly-empty files and can't remember which one holds the one function you actually wrote.

contentSections.question: Does creating a full folder structure (utils/, components/, helpers/, services/) before you have enough code to justify it make a small, early project easier or harder to work in?
contentSections.hint: Think about what you're actually optimizing for — fewer lines to scroll, or fewer files to remember the location of.
contentSections.answer: Usually harder, at that stage. With only a handful of real pieces of code, spreading them across many mostly-empty folders means you now have to remember which folder holds which one small thing, instead of just scrolling a short file. The folder structure isn't wrong forever — it becomes genuinely useful once there's enough real code that grouping it saves more than it costs. Premature structure optimizes for a project size you don't have yet.

contentSections.body: A reasonable middle ground: start in one file, and split out a specific piece the moment you can name the concrete reason — "this function is used in three places and I keep scrolling to find it," or "these forty lines are a clearly separate concern from the rest of this file." That's a real, earned reason. "Big projects have folders" on its own isn't.
Splitting too early costs just as much as splitting too late — both trade a real problem you have for navigation overhead you don't need yet.

title: Splitting code into modules with a reason
description: Splitting a file into modules means moving related code together and unrelated code apart, then connecting the pieces deliberately with export and import — not just cutting a big file into smaller, equally-tangled ones.

learningObjectives.text: Split a function out of one file into its own module using export/import
Distinguish a genuine split (by responsibility) from an arbitrary one (by line count)

contentSections.title: Splitting by what code is responsible for

contentSections.body: A 900-line app.js has login code, discount-calculation code, and API-fetching code all mixed together. "Split it up" could mean a lot of things — the useful version splits it by what each piece is actually responsible for, not by where line 300 happens to fall.

contentSections.problem: Move the discount calculation out of a large app.js into its own module, discount.js, and use it from app.js.

steps.label: Identify the self-contained piece
steps.why: This function doesn't depend on login state, API responses, or anything else in the file — a clean sign it can genuinely stand alone.

steps.label: Move it to its own file and export it
steps.why: `export` marks this function as something other files are allowed to use — without it, the function would be trapped inside discount.js, invisible to everything else.

steps.label: Import it where it's actually used
steps.work:
// app.js
import { applyDiscount } from './discount.js';
steps.why: This one line replaces the entire function body that used to live inline — app.js now says clearly "I use applyDiscount, defined elsewhere" instead of burying the logic in the middle of unrelated code.

steps.label: Use it exactly as before
steps.work: const finalPrice = applyDiscount(100, 10);
steps.why: The call site doesn't change at all — splitting the file changed where the code lives, not how it behaves or how you use it.

faded.problem: Move a validateEmail function out of app.js into its own module, validation.js.

blanks.why: export is what makes the function usable from other files — without it, the code is stuck inside validation.js alone.
The path './validation.js' points at the file relative to app.js — matching the export's name exactly.
Where the function lives changed; how you call it didn't.

contentSections.procedure: Identify a self-contained piece of code, move it to its own file, export it there, and import it wherever it's used — the call sites don't change, only where the definition physically lives.

contentSections.body: export marks a piece of code as usable elsewhere; import brings it in where it's needed — the split is about responsibility, not line count.

contentSections.title: A split that doesn't actually help

contentSections.body: A teammate "organizes" a 900-line app.js by cutting it into part1.js (lines 1-300), part2.js (lines 301-600), and part3.js (lines 601-900). It's technically three files now.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways to split the same 900-line file: (A) part1.js/part2.js/part3.js, cut at arbitrary line numbers, still mixing login, discount, and API code across all three; (B) login.js, discount.js, api.js, each containing everything related to exactly one responsibility.
contentSections.question: Which split actually makes the discount bug from lesson 1 easier to find?

options.label: B — discount.js contains only discount-related code, so there's nowhere else to look
A — three smaller files are easier to search than one big one, regardless of what's in each
Neither — splitting doesn't change how easy a bug is to find

feedback.b: Right. Splitting by responsibility means discount.js is exactly and only where discount code lives — finding the bug means opening one specific, correctly-named file, not guessing which of three arbitrarily-sized chunks it landed in.
feedback.a: Smaller files aren't inherently easier to search if each one still mixes several unrelated concerns — you'd still have to scan all three, just in three separate searches instead of one. The size went down; the actual confusion didn't.
feedback.neither: Splitting genuinely can help — the point isn't that splitting never helps, it's that splitting by an arbitrary boundary (line count) doesn't get you the benefit that splitting by responsibility does.

contentSections.concept: A split by line count is organization theater — it looks like structure without providing the actual benefit, because related code can still be scattered anywhere. A split by responsibility (what a piece of code is actually for) means a file's name tells you what's inside it, and a bug related to one responsibility has exactly one place to look.

contentSections.body: Splitting by responsibility (what code does) actually helps. Splitting by line count alone just moves the same tangle into more files.

title: Naming files and folders for the person who arrives later
description: A good file or folder name lets someone guess what's inside before opening it — the "person who arrives later" is very often you, in a few months, having forgotten everything about today.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a file or folder name communicates its actual contents
Choose a clear name over a clever or vague one for a real file's purpose

contentSections.title: The name is a promise about what's inside

contentSections.body: You open a project you built four months ago, looking for the code that validates a signup form. The files are named: `utils.js`, `helpers2.js`, `stuff.js`, `final.js`, `main2.js`. None of these tell you anything. You end up opening all five, one by one, to find it.

contentSections.scenario: Five real file names from the same project, holding: signup-form validation logic, date-formatting helpers, the main app entry point, discount-calculation logic, and a leftover experimental file nobody uses anymore.
contentSections.question: Which naming choice below actually helps you find the signup validation code four months from now, without opening every file?

options.label: validateSignupForm.js — names the exact responsibility, guessable without opening it
utils.js — a name generic enough that almost any function could plausibly live there
final2.js — implies a version history with no information about contents

feedback.specific: Right. A name like validateSignupForm.js is a direct, honest label — it tells you what's inside before you open it, which is the entire point of naming something in the first place. Four months from now, you can find it by guessing the name, not by opening five files.
feedback.generic: "utils" is one of the most common vague names in real projects, and it's vague precisely because it could describe almost anything — a date formatter, a validator, a random helper, all equally plausible. A generic name gives you zero information to search by.
feedback.versioned: "final2" (or final, finalReal, finalActually) tells you nothing about what's inside — only that at some point there was a first version and someone made another one. It's the file-naming version of the manual versioning problem from the git module: information about history, none about content.

contentSections.concept: A file's name is effectively a promise about its contents, read before the file is opened. A name specific to what the code actually does (validateSignupForm.js) keeps that promise; a name generic enough to fit almost anything (utils.js, helpers.js, stuff.js) or one describing history instead of content (final2.js) breaks it, forcing anyone looking — including you, later — to open files just to find out what's in them.

contentSections.body: This applies to folders exactly the same way, one level up: a folder named `components/` next to one named `misc/` tells you the second one is where things went when nobody wanted to think about where they actually belonged. It's not that generic names are always wrong — a genuinely general-purpose helper (say, a function used by five completely unrelated parts of the app) might legitimately live in something like `utils.js`. The problem is using "utils" as the default answer for anything you didn't want to name properly.
A file name is a promise about what's inside, read before anyone opens it — generic and vague names break that promise, specific ones keep it.

contentSections.title: Consistency is its own kind of clarity

contentSections.body: A project has `userProfile.js`, `UserSettings.js`, `user-preferences.js`, and `USER_STATS.JS` — four files about the same general subject, four completely different naming styles. Finding the right one means remembering, or guessing, which style was used that particular day.

contentSections.scenario: The same project's file names, all describing user-related features, but each written in a different casing style: camelCase, PascalCase, kebab-case, and SCREAMING_CASE.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually make a project harder to navigate over time? Select all that apply.

items.label: Using four different casing styles across files about the same kind of thing, with no pattern to which is used when
Not being able to predict a file's exact name before searching for it, because the style varies
Picking one consistent casing style and using it for every file in the project, whichever style it is
Choosing names that describe what's inside a file, regardless of casing style

explanation.inconsistent_casing: This is a real cost — every new file forces a fresh decision with no pattern to follow, and every search for an existing file means guessing which style it happened to use.
explanation.unpredictable_search: This is the concrete downstream cost of the inconsistency: you can't type a filename from memory with confidence, because the same project uses several different conventions.
explanation.any_one_style: A single consistent style, whichever one it is, removes the guessing entirely — camelCase everywhere is exactly as fine as kebab-case everywhere, as long as it's the same choice throughout.
explanation.descriptive_names: Descriptive naming is a separate, good thing from lesson content earlier in this pod — it doesn't create a problem on its own, and pairs fine with any consistent casing style.

contentSections.body: It matters far less which naming convention you pick than that you pick one and use it everywhere — consistency is what makes a name predictable.

title: Configuration and the values that change per environment
description: A value that changes depending on where the code runs — a database address, an API key, a feature flag — belongs in configuration, kept separate from and out of the code itself.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a value that should live in configuration rather than hardcoded in the code
Explain why environment-specific values in code cause real failures when moved between environments

contentSections.title: The value that's right here, wrong there

contentSections.body: Your project works perfectly on your laptop. You deploy it, and it immediately breaks — the API URL is hardcoded as `http://localhost:3000`, which means something specific and real on your machine and means nothing at all on a live server.

contentSections.scenario: A function calls `fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/users')` directly, written into the code. It works while developing locally. Deployed to a real server, every request fails.
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong here, and what does it reveal about hardcoding this value?

options.label: localhost:3000 refers to "this machine, port 3000" — meaningful on a laptop during development, meaningless once deployed somewhere else entirely
The URL is spelled incorrectly
fetch() doesn't work at all once a project is deployed

feedback.meaning_changes: Right. "localhost" isn't a placeholder that happens to be wrong — it's a genuinely correct address, but only for whichever machine is running the code at that moment. Baked directly into the code, it silently stops meaning anything useful the instant the code runs somewhere else, which is exactly what deploying does.
feedback.typo: The URL is spelled exactly right — the problem isn't a mistake in typing it, it's that the correct value for one environment (your laptop) is a wrong value for another (a live server).
feedback.fetch_broken: fetch() works fine on a deployed server — the actual failure is that it's being told to ask localhost:3000, which on a live server either means nothing or means something completely different than intended.

contentSections.mechanism: Any value whose correct answer depends on *where* the code is currently running — a local vs. live API address, a test vs. real database, a development vs. production API key — will be right in exactly one place and silently wrong everywhere else if it's hardcoded directly into the code. The fix isn't a better hardcoded value; it's not hardcoding it at all.

contentSections.body: Configuration is the practice of pulling these values out of the code and into something that changes per environment — commonly environment variables, read at runtime instead of written directly into a file. The code says `fetch(process.env.API_URL + '/api/users')`; what `API_URL` actually equals is set separately, differently, on your laptop versus on the live server, without touching the code itself at all.
A hardcoded value that's correct on your machine can be silently wrong everywhere else — configuration keeps the code the same while letting the value change per environment.

contentSections.title: Secrets are configuration too, and extra sensitive

contentSections.body: An API key hardcoded directly in a file has all the same environment problem as the localhost URL — plus a second one. The moment that file is committed to git (from the version-control module) or just glanced at by anyone with access, the key is exposed.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways of holding an API key: (A) directly written into the code as a quoted string, (B) read from an environment variable at runtime, with the real value stored in a `.env` file that's listed in `.gitignore` and never committed.
contentSections.question: Beyond the environment-mismatch problem, what does option A specifically risk that option B avoids?

options.label: The key becomes visible to anyone who can read the code — including permanently, in git history, once committed
Option A is slower to run than option B
Nothing extra — both carry exactly the same risk

feedback.exposure: Right. A key written directly into a file is exposed to anyone who can read that file — a teammate, anyone who clones the repo, and (as the git module covered) permanently, in history, if it's ever committed, even briefly. Reading it from an environment variable, with the real value kept in an ignored .env file, means the actual secret never appears in the code or the repository at all.
feedback.speed: There's no meaningful runtime speed difference between reading a hardcoded string and reading an environment variable — the real difference is entirely about exposure, not performance.
feedback.same: The two aren't equivalent — option A puts the actual secret value directly into a file that's likely to be shared, committed, or read by more people than intended. Option B keeps the real value entirely outside the code, in a file specifically excluded from version control.

contentSections.concept: Secrets are configuration with an extra requirement: not just "changes per environment" but "must never be visible in the code or committed to the repository at all." The pattern is the same as any other config value — read from an environment variable at runtime — plus a .gitignore entry that keeps the actual value out of git entirely.

contentSections.body: Secrets are configuration values with a stricter rule: never in the code, never committed — read from the environment, with the real value kept out of git entirely.

title: A README that lets someone else run it
description: A README's job is to get a project from a fresh clone to actually running, in someone else's hands, without them having to ask you anything.

learningObjectives.text: Write a README that lets a stranger run the project from a fresh clone
Identify what a README needs beyond a project description to actually be useful

contentSections.title: A description isn't the same as instructions

contentSections.body: A README reads: "A tool that tracks daily symptoms and shows trends over time. Built with JavaScript." It's accurate. A stranger clones the repo, opens it, and has genuinely no idea what command to run, what to install first, or what a `.env` file they're supposed to create should even contain.

contentSections.scenario: Two READMEs for the same project. README A: a paragraph describing what the app does and why it was built. README B: the same paragraph, plus "1. Run `npm install`. 2. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and add your own API key. 3. Run `npm run dev`. 4. Open `http://localhost:3000`."
contentSections.question: A stranger clones this project fresh. Which README actually gets it running on their machine?

options.label: B — it gives the exact sequence of commands and setup steps, not just a description of the end result
A — a clear description is usually enough for someone who already knows the tech stack
Neither — anyone competent enough to clone a repo can figure out the rest

feedback.b: Right. Knowing what a project does doesn't tell a stranger which command installs its dependencies, which environment variables it needs, or which command starts it — those are specific, project-by-project facts that only exist in the README (or in your head, which doesn't help anyone else). B is the difference between describing a destination and giving directions.
feedback.a: Even a reader who knows the tech stack in general has no way to guess this specific project's exact commands, required environment variables, or file structure — those vary project to project and have to be written down explicitly.
feedback.neither: "Figure it out" is exactly the cost a good README removes — every minute a stranger (or future-you) spends guessing setup steps is a minute a written README would have saved outright.

contentSections.concept: A description tells someone what a project is; instructions tell them how to actually get it running on their own machine. A README needs both, but the instructions — install, configure, run — are the part that's actually specific to this project and can't be guessed, and they're the part most often left out.

contentSections.body: A genuinely useful README's setup section is close to a checklist: what to install first (and how), what environment variables are required and where to get real values for them (or a `.env.example` file showing the shape without real secrets), the exact command that starts the project, and what you should see once it's working. Each of these is a place a stranger — or you, coming back in six months — would otherwise have to guess or dig through code to find.
A README's job is getting someone from a fresh clone to a running project — a description of what it does is necessary but not sufficient for that.

contentSections.title: Writing it as if you don't already know

contentSections.body: You write your own README in five minutes, from memory, and it feels complete. The real test isn't whether it feels complete to you — you already know every step by heart. It's whether someone who's never seen this project could actually follow it.

contentSections.question: You've just written a README from memory. What's a more reliable check that it actually works than reading it back to yourself?
contentSections.hint: You already know all the steps — reading your own README won't reveal what you silently assumed the reader already knows.
contentSections.answer: Actually try to follow it, ideally on a genuinely fresh setup (a new folder, or asking someone else to try) — clone the repo using only the README, and see where you get stuck or have to guess. Every place you have to think "oh, I forgot I also needed to..." is a gap the README needs to close. Reading your own instructions back to yourself doesn't catch this, because you already know the parts you left out.

contentSections.body: The real test of a README isn't whether it reads well to you — it's whether someone with none of your context can actually follow it and end up with a running project.

title: Practice — Restructure Seven Messy Projects
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a messy project description, decide what actually needs restructuring and why.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific structural problem in a described messy project

contentSections.title: Seven messy projects, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: when a file has genuinely outgrown itself, splitting by responsibility versus by line count, naming that communicates versus naming that doesn't, configuration that should never be hardcoded, and a README that's a description instead of instructions.
The same real question, every time: does this structure make the next change easier to find and make safely, or is it just organization for its own sake?

title: Lab — Restructure Your Project and Write Its README
description: Take a real, messier-than-it-should-be project and give it a genuine structural pass — split by responsibility, name things clearly, pull environment-specific values out of the code, and write a README a total stranger could follow.

learningObjectives.text: Split a tangled file into modules organized by responsibility
Move environment-specific and secret values out of the code into configuration
Write a README that gets a stranger from a fresh clone to a running project

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Pick a real project of yours that's grown past a single tidy file — something from earlier in this track is ideal. By the end of this lab, someone who has never seen it could clone it and get it running, using nothing but what's actually in the repository.

contentSections.title: Restructure your project and write its README
contentSections.brief: Take a real project that's outgrown a single file. Split it into modules organized by what each piece is actually responsible for, name everything so it's guessable without opening it, pull any hardcoded environment-specific or secret values into configuration, and write a README a stranger could actually follow from a fresh clone.

stages.checkpoint: Each new file has one clear responsibility you could name in a sentence, and the project still runs exactly as before.

stages.title: Rename for the person arriving later
stages.instructions: Review every file and folder name in the project. Rename anything vague (utils, stuff, final, misc) to something that describes its actual contents, and make sure the whole project uses one consistent naming style throughout.
stages.checkpoint: Every file's name would let a stranger guess what's inside it without opening it, and the casing style is consistent project-wide.

stages.title: Move environment-specific values into configuration
stages.instructions: Find any hardcoded value that would be wrong in a different environment (a localhost URL, a real API key, anything similar) and move it into an environment variable. Create a `.env.example` showing the required shape with placeholder values, and confirm your real `.env` is listed in .gitignore.
stages.checkpoint: No environment-specific value or real secret is hardcoded anywhere in the committed code, and .env.example documents what's needed without exposing real values.

stages.title: Write and test the README
stages.instructions: Write a README with a short description plus exact, numbered setup steps: install, configure (referencing .env.example), and run. Then actually test it — either in a genuinely fresh clone, or by following it step by step yourself as if you'd never seen the project before, and fix anything you have to silently fill in from memory.
stages.checkpoint: You've actually followed your own README start to finish and it produced a running project with no unwritten steps.

rubric.criterion: The split is by responsibility, not line count
rubric.meets: Each new file holds one nameable responsibility, and the project behaves exactly as it did before the split.

rubric.criterion: Names are specific and consistent
rubric.meets: No vague names (utils/stuff/misc/final) survive, and casing style is consistent across the whole project.

rubric.criterion: No environment-specific value is hardcoded
rubric.meets: URLs, keys, and similar values are read from environment variables, with .env correctly excluded from git.

rubric.criterion: .env.example documents what's needed
rubric.meets: A stranger can see exactly which environment variables are required, with placeholder (not real) values.

rubric.criterion: The README was actually tested, not just written
rubric.meets: You personally followed it start to finish and it produced a running project with nothing silently skipped.

contentSections.body: A project a stranger can actually clone and run, using only the README, is the real deliverable — everything else in this module was in service of that.

title: Checkpoint — Organising a Project
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Checking Your Own Work, two reaching back into Version Control and Getting Data From Elsewhere. Ungraded, untimed.

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Organising a Project

questions.from: This module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: What's the actual, concrete sign that a single-file project has outgrown that structure?

options.label: A pointable cost — scrolling past unrelated code, tangled features, or colliding changes — not size alone
Reaching exactly 500 lines
Having more than one function in the file

questions.explanation: The real signal is a concrete friction you can point to, not a line-count threshold — a file with 500 unrelated lines and a file with 500 lines all doing one clear job are very different situations.

questions.from: This module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: Splitting a 900-line file into part1.js, part2.js, part3.js by arbitrary line ranges — does this actually help find a bug in one feature?

options.label: Not really — related code can still be scattered across all three files; only splitting by responsibility fixes that
Yes — three smaller files are always easier to search than one big one
Yes, but only if each file is under 200 lines

questions.explanation: A split by line count doesn't group related code together — it just spreads the same tangle across more files. Splitting by responsibility (what code does) is what actually helps.

questions.from: This module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: Why does hardcoding `http://localhost:3000` directly into a fetch call break once the project is deployed?

options.label: localhost refers to "this machine" — correct on your laptop, meaningless once the code runs somewhere else
fetch() itself stops working once deployed
The URL has a typo

questions.explanation: The value is genuinely correct in one specific environment and silently wrong in every other — the fix is reading it from configuration instead of hardcoding it.

questions.from: This module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: What makes a README's setup section actually useful to a stranger, beyond a description of what the project does?

options.label: Exact, specific instructions — install, configure, run — that can't be guessed from a general description
A longer, more detailed description of the app's purpose
Screenshots of the finished app

questions.explanation: Knowing what a project does doesn't tell a stranger the specific commands and environment variables this particular project needs — that has to be written down explicitly as instructions.

questions.from: Previous module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: what's wrong with a test using expect(result).toBeDefined() to check a function's output?

options.label: It would pass even if the function returned a completely wrong value — it only checks something came back
toBeDefined() is invalid syntax
Nothing — it's a perfectly strong assertion

questions.explanation: toBeDefined() only confirms a value exists, not that it's correct — a broken function could still pass it, giving false confidence.

questions.from: Previous module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: what's the concrete way to prove a test would actually catch a real bug?

options.label: Temporarily break the real code it tests and confirm the test fails, then revert and confirm it passes again
Run the test twice in a row
Check that the test has a descriptive name

questions.explanation: Watching a test go red on deliberately broken code, then green again on the real code, is the only real proof it's checking something meaningful.

questions.from: Previous module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: why is testing only the happy-path input not enough?

options.label: It's the case every implementation is naturally built to handle first — edge cases (zero, negative, boundary) are where bugs actually tend to hide
The happy path is actually the hardest case to get right
It isn't a real limitation — happy-path testing alone is fully sufficient

questions.explanation: The happy path is the least likely case to reveal a bug precisely because it's the case naturally handled first — edges are where implementations disagree about correct behavior.

questions.from: Previous module — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: a boundary bug like `age > 65` instead of `age >= 65` — why do tests at age 30 and age 70 both fail to catch it?

options.label: Both sides of the boundary give the same result whether the code uses > or >= — only testing the exact boundary value (65) reveals the difference
Those two ages are outside the function's valid range
> and >= always produce identical results for any input

questions.explanation: Away from the exact boundary, > and >= behave identically — the bug is only visible by testing the precise threshold value itself.

questions.from: Three modules back — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: why does deleting a leaked secret from the current file not fully fix the leak?

options.label: The secret is still visible in the earlier commit that first added it — it needs to be rotated, not just edited out
It does fully fix it, since only the current file matters
Deleted secrets can never be recovered from git history

questions.explanation: Every commit is a permanent snapshot — the earlier commit with the secret is still in history, recoverable regardless of later edits.

questions.from: Four modules back — Getting Data From Elsewhere
questions.prompt: From Getting Data From Elsewhere: why can't a secret API key be safely hidden inside frontend JavaScript?

options.label: Everything sent to the browser is fully downloaded and readable by anyone who opens dev tools
It can be hidden safely with an unclear variable name
Browsers automatically encrypt all JavaScript before running it

questions.explanation: Frontend code is fully delivered to and readable in the browser — a real secret has to live on a server the browser never directly sees.
