title: Where to start in an unfamiliar project
description: Reading every file top to bottom is the slowest possible way into an unfamiliar project — starting from the README and the entry point, then following one real thing through it, gets you oriented far faster.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a project's entry point as a starting place for reading unfamiliar code
Explain why reading files in alphabetical or arbitrary order is an inefficient way to understand a project

contentSections.title: Not every file, and not in file-explorer order

contentSections.body: You're asked to fix a small bug in a project you've never seen — forty files, no idea where anything is. The instinct is to open the file explorer and start reading from the top: components/, then config/, then lib/, alphabetically, hoping it'll click eventually. Forty minutes in, you've read a lot of code and still don't know where the bug you're supposed to fix even lives.

contentSections.scenario: Four ways people actually try to get oriented in an unfamiliar project: (1) reading every file top to bottom in file-explorer order, (2) reading the README, then finding the entry point (the file that actually starts the app), then following what it calls, (3) opening files at random hoping something looks familiar, (4) asking someone to just explain the whole thing verbally before touching any code.
contentSections.question: Which approach actually gets you oriented fastest for a real, unfamiliar task — like fixing one specific bug?

options.label: Reading the README, then the entry point, then following what it calls — building a map from the one place every request or run actually starts
Reading every file top to bottom in file-explorer order
Opening files at random hoping something looks familiar

feedback.entry: Right. The entry point is the one place every request, click, or run of the program genuinely starts — following what it calls, and what those calls call, builds a real map of how the pieces connect, in the order they actually execute, instead of the arbitrary order they happen to sit in a file browser.
feedback.alphabetical: File-explorer order has nothing to do with how the code actually runs — a file near the top alphabetically might be a rarely-used helper, while the file that actually starts everything could be buried near the bottom. You'd read a lot without learning how anything connects.
feedback.random: Random exploration occasionally gets lucky, but there's no reason to expect it — you have no way to know if what you're looking at is central to how the app works or a rarely-used edge case, and no systematic way to build up a real map.

contentSections.concept: A project's entry point — the file that actually starts running when the app launches, or the specific handler a request first hits — is the one place guaranteed to matter, because everything the program does starts from there. Reading outward from it, following what it calls, builds real understanding of how pieces connect; reading files in whatever order they happen to be listed builds none of that.

contentSections.body: A useful first pass, in order: read the README (if there is one) for what the project does and how to run it — lesson 5 of the last module covered why this exists. Find the entry point — often named something like `main.js`, `index.js`, `app.js`, or named in the README's "run" instructions. Skim what it calls, without chasing every branch yet, just to see the shape: does it start a server, render a page, run a script top to bottom? That shape is the map everything else in the project hangs off of.
The entry point is the one place guaranteed to matter — everything the program does starts from there, which makes it the fastest place to start reading from.

contentSections.title: You don't need to understand everything before you start

contentSections.body: Forty files, and the instinct is that you need to fully understand all of them before touching anything — otherwise how would you know you're not breaking something? That instinct, taken seriously, means never actually starting.

contentSections.question: You've been asked to fix one specific bug in an unfamiliar 40-file project. Do you need to fully understand all 40 files before you can safely make the fix?
contentSections.hint: Think about how much of the entry point's territory the specific bug you're fixing actually touches.
contentSections.answer: No — you need to understand the specific path the bug's behavior travels through, which is usually a small fraction of the whole project. Most real changes touch one feature's worth of code, not the entire codebase. Trying to fully understand all 40 files before starting is exactly the kind of scope that guarantees you never start — the actual skill (covered in the next few lessons) is following one specific thing through the code, not reading everything.

contentSections.body: This reframes the whole module: "reading someone else's code" doesn't mean reading it all — it means being able to follow one real thing (a bug, a feature, a specific behavior) through however much of the project it actually touches, and stopping there. That's a genuinely learnable, bounded skill. "Understand the entire codebase first" is not a real requirement anyone actually meets, even people who've worked on a project for years.
You don't need to understand a whole unfamiliar project — you need to follow the one specific thing you're working on through however much of it that actually touches.

title: Following one thing through the code
description: Pick one concrete, observable behavior — a button click, a specific output — and trace it step by step from where it starts to where it ends, instead of trying to absorb the whole file.

learningObjectives.text: Trace a specific behavior through multiple functions or files to its source

contentSections.title: Pick a thread and pull it

contentSections.body: A shop page shows "Free shipping over $50" and it's wrong — the message shows even on a $30 order. You don't know this codebase. Rather than reading the whole file, you pick exactly one thread: where does that message's text actually come from?

contentSections.problem: Trace where the "Free shipping over $50" message comes from, in an unfamiliar checkout.js file, to find why it's showing incorrectly.

steps.label: Find the literal text on screen
steps.work: Search the project for the exact string "Free shipping"
steps.why: The literal text is a concrete, searchable anchor — far more specific than trying to guess which function might be relevant.

steps.label: See what decides whether it shows
steps.why: This tells you the message itself isn't the bug — a variable, showFreeShippingBanner, decides whether it's shown at all. That's the next thread to pull.

steps.label: Find where that variable is set
steps.work:
// search for showFreeShippingBanner:
const showFreeShippingBanner = cartTotal >= 0;
steps.why: This is the actual bug: comparing against 0 instead of 50. The fix is narrowed to one specific line, found by following the thread instead of reading the whole file.

steps.label: Confirm nothing else sets it elsewhere
steps.work: Search the whole project for showFreeShippingBanner one more time
steps.why: A quick check that this is the only place the value is set — otherwise there could be a second, conflicting assignment somewhere else that would undo your fix.

faded.problem: Trace why a "Welcome back!" message is showing for a user who has never logged in before, in an unfamiliar auth.js file.

blanks.prompt: First move — find the literal text
blanks.answer: Search the project for the exact string "Welcome back"
blanks.why: A specific, searchable string is a far more precise starting anchor than guessing which function is relevant.

blanks.prompt: What you're looking for once you find it
blanks.answer: The condition or variable that decides whether it's shown
blanks.why: The message's existence isn't the bug — whatever controls when it's shown is where the real logic (and the bug) actually lives.

blanks.prompt: Once you find that condition, what's the next step
blanks.answer: Trace where that condition's value actually comes from
blanks.why: Following the thread one more link — from "what decides this" to "where does that thing get its value" — is usually where the real bug is found.

contentSections.procedure: Start from something concrete and searchable (exact text, an error message, a specific behavior), find what controls it, then follow that one thread backward until you reach the actual source — not the whole surrounding file.

contentSections.body: Start from something concrete and searchable — exact text, a specific behavior — and follow it one link at a time, rather than reading everything around it.

contentSections.title: Following data is often clearer than following logic

contentSections.body: Sometimes the clearest thread to pull isn't "what controls this behavior" but "where does this specific value actually come from" — following a piece of data backward through the functions that touch it.

contentSections.question: A cart total displays as $NaN. Put these tracing steps in the order that actually leads to the bug, starting from the broken display:
steps: Find where $NaN is rendered on screen and identify the variable being displayed
Find where that variable is calculated
Check each value that calculation depends on
Find the one input that isn't actually a number (a form field's raw, unconverted string value)
contentSections.explanation: Tracing backward from the visible symptom (the rendered $NaN) to the calculation, then to its inputs, is what actually narrows the search — jumping straight to "the math must be wrong" without checking the inputs first would miss the real cause, which (per the storing-data and JavaScript modules) is very often a string that was never converted to a number.

contentSections.body: Following one specific thread — a behavior, or a piece of data — backward to its source is what turns an unfamiliar file into something you can actually navigate.

title: Using search and jump-to-definition properly
description: A code editor's search and "jump to definition" are the real tools for navigating unfamiliar code — searching by the right thing, and following a function's actual definition instead of guessing what it does from its name.

learningObjectives.text: Choose an effective search term when looking for something in an unfamiliar codebase
Use jump-to-definition to find where a function actually does what it does

contentSections.title: What you search for matters more than the tool

contentSections.body: You're looking for where a discount gets applied in an unfamiliar project. You search for "discount" and get 140 results across 30 files — variable names, comments, unrelated features that happen to mention discounts. The search worked; the search term didn't.

contentSections.scenario: Searching an unfamiliar project for where a specific bug lives — a discount showing as 0% when it should be 10%. Four possible search terms: "discount" (140 results), "applyDiscount" (the actual function name, visible in a stack trace or error, 3 results), "0%" (the literal wrong output, unlikely to appear in source code at all), "bug" (0 relevant results).
contentSections.question: Which search term is actually likely to get you to the real code fastest?

options.label: "applyDiscount" — a specific function name gives a small, relevant result set instead of hundreds of loosely-related hits
"discount" — casting the widest net possible is always the safest search
"0%" — searching for the exact wrong output you're seeing

feedback.specific: Right. A specific identifier — a function name, a variable name, an error message's exact text — narrows results to the places that actually matter. "discount" is too broad (comments, unrelated variables, unrelated features), while a real function name like applyDiscount is precise and rare enough to point straight at the relevant code.
feedback.wide: A wide net feels safer, but in practice it just means wading through more irrelevant results by hand — the same scrolling-and-guessing problem this whole module is trying to avoid, just inside search results instead of files.
feedback.output: The literal wrong number ("0%") almost never appears anywhere in the source code itself — it's a *result* of running the code, not text that exists in a file. Searching for computed output is usually a dead end; searching for the code that produces it (a function or variable name) is what actually works.

contentSections.concept: A search term is only as useful as how uniquely it points at the relevant code. Specific identifiers — function names, variable names, exact error message text — narrow a search to what matters. Generic words and computed output values tend to return either far too much or nothing useful at all.

contentSections.body: Where do specific identifiers come from, in an unfamiliar project, before you know any of the function names? Error messages and stack traces (from the errors module) often name the exact function where something failed. The visible text on screen, searched for directly, often leads to the component or template that renders it, which then names the variables and functions feeding it. Each of these gives you a specific, searchable term — the goal is always narrowing from "somewhere in this project" to "this one function, in this one file."
A specific identifier — a function name, an exact error message, real on-screen text — narrows a search to what matters. Generic words return noise.

contentSections.title: Jump-to-definition instead of guessing from the name

contentSections.body: You find a call to `calculateShipping(cart)`. The name suggests what it does — but names can be wrong, outdated, or incomplete, and guessing from a name instead of actually looking is exactly how a small change turns into an unexpected bug.

contentSections.scenario: A function named `calculateShipping(cart)` is called in checkout.js. Based on the name alone, it seems safe to assume it just computes a shipping cost and returns a number.
contentSections.question: You use jump-to-definition (or search for the function's actual definition) and find it also silently updates a `lastCalculated` timestamp on the cart object as a side effect, undocumented in the name. Why does this matter for a change you're about to make?

options.label: Calling this function anywhere new — even just to check a shipping cost — would now also silently change cart state, which the name gives no hint of
It doesn't matter — the function's name is what defines its behavior, not its actual code
This is a bug in the function that should be ignored while reading code

feedback.hidden_side_effect: Right. A function's actual behavior is whatever its code does, not whatever its name suggests — calling calculateShipping anywhere new, expecting only a returned number, would also silently mutate the cart's timestamp, an effect the name never mentions. This is exactly the kind of thing that only shows up by reading the real definition, not by trusting the name.
feedback.name_defines: Names are written by humans and can drift out of sync with what the code actually does, especially in an unfamiliar project you didn't write — the real behavior is always in the code itself, which is why jump-to-definition matters more than guessing from a name.
feedback.ignore: Whether or not it's good practice for the original author to have hidden a side effect in a function like this, it's real, current behavior you need to know about before using or changing the function — reading code means dealing with what's actually there, not what should ideally be there.

contentSections.mechanism: Jump-to-definition takes you directly to a function's real, current implementation — the only reliable source of truth for what it actually does, including side effects, edge-case handling, or outdated behavior a name doesn't capture. Guessing from a name is a shortcut that works until the one time it doesn't, silently.

contentSections.body: A function's name is a hint, not a guarantee — jump-to-definition shows you what it actually does, including anything the name doesn't mention.

title: Making a small change safely
description: In unfamiliar code, the safe move is the smallest change that fixes the one thing you're looking at — verified before and after — not a wider cleanup you weren't asked for.

learningObjectives.text: Scope a change in unfamiliar code to the minimum needed to fix the identified issue
Verify a change in unfamiliar code didn't affect anything beyond its intended scope

contentSections.title: Fix the one thing, not everything you notice

contentSections.body: You've traced the free-shipping bug from lesson 2 to one line: `cartTotal >= 0` should be `cartTotal >= 50`. While you're in that file, you also notice the variable is named inconsistently elsewhere, a comment is outdated, and a nearby function could probably be simplified. It's tempting to fix all of it while you're already there.

contentSections.scenario: You were asked to fix one specific bug: the free-shipping threshold. While in the file, you also notice three unrelated things that could be improved.
contentSections.question: In an unfamiliar codebase you don't yet deeply understand, what's the risk of fixing all four things in one change?

options.label: Each unrelated change is its own chance to break something you don't yet understand well enough to be confident about — and if something breaks, it's harder to tell which of the four changes caused it
There's no real risk — more improvements in one change is always better
The risk is purely about the time it takes, not about correctness

feedback.risk_scope: Right. In code you don't yet deeply understand, every additional unrelated change is an additional chance to break something in a way you're not positioned to catch — and if something does break, a change that touched four unrelated things is much harder to debug than four small changes, each of which can be checked and reasoned about on its own.
feedback.no_risk: More changes bundled together isn't automatically better, especially here — the entire premise of this module is that you don't yet have full context on this codebase, which is exactly when small, scoped changes are safest.
feedback.time_only: The real risk isn't just time — it's that bundling unrelated changes together makes it much harder to identify which one caused a problem if something breaks, and increases the chance you introduce a bug in code you don't fully understand yet.

contentSections.concept: The safe move in unfamiliar code is the smallest change that actually fixes the thing you were asked to fix — not because the other improvements aren't real, but because each additional unrelated change is an additional risk in code you don't yet have full context on, and makes any resulting bug harder to isolate. Noticing other issues is useful (write them down, maybe raise them separately) — bundling them into the same change isn't.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the version-control module: a small, scoped change makes for a small, scoped commit with a message that says exactly what it does — "fix free-shipping threshold from $0 to $50" — instead of a sprawling commit mixing a real fix with three unrelated cleanups nobody asked for and nobody can easily review or revert independently.
The safe change in unfamiliar code is the smallest one that actually fixes what you set out to fix — not everything you happen to notice along the way.

contentSections.title: Verify before and after, not just after

contentSections.body: You make the fix, it looks right, and you move on. A day later someone reports the free-shipping banner now shows for every order, including a $5 one. Confirming a fix "looks right" by eye is not the same as verifying it actually behaves correctly.

contentSections.scenario: Ways to verify a small change to unfamiliar code actually works and hasn't broken anything nearby: reading the changed line and confirming it looks correct; running the specific behavior you fixed and confirming it's now right; running the behavior you fixed for a case that should NOT trigger it (e.g. a $30 order); running the project's existing test suite, if one exists.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually give you real evidence the fix is correct and safe? Select all that apply.

items.label: Running the specific case you fixed and confirming the correct behavior now happens
Running a case that should NOT trigger the fixed behavior, confirming it correctly still doesn't
Running the project's existing test suite, if one exists, to check nothing else broke
Reading the changed line and confirming it looks correct, without actually running anything

explanation.run_fixed_case: This is direct evidence the specific bug is actually fixed, not just that the code reads correctly to you.
explanation.run_negative_case: This is exactly what would have caught the "free shipping now shows for every order" regression — checking that the fix didn't overcorrect into a new, opposite bug.
explanation.run_tests: An existing test suite (from the testing module) is the fastest way to check the change didn't silently break something else in the project you're not even aware of yet.
explanation.reading_only: Reading a line and confirming it looks correct is a reasonable first check, but it's not verification — it's exactly the same kind of confidence a weak test like toBeDefined() gives: it feels like checking, without actually confirming real behavior.

contentSections.body: "It looks right" isn't verification — actually running the fixed case, a case that shouldn't trigger it, and the existing tests is what confirms a change is genuinely safe.

title: Knowing when you don't understand it yet
description: Recognizing code (it looks familiar) and understanding it (you could predict what it does, or safely change it) are two different things — and mistaking the first for the second is where confident, unsafe changes come from.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish recognizing code from actually understanding it
Identify a genuine test of whether you understand a piece of unfamiliar code

contentSections.title: Recognizing isn't the same as understanding

contentSections.body: You read a function using .filter() and .map(), both familiar from earlier in this track. It feels understandable — the syntax is recognizable. But asked "what would this return if the cart were empty?", you realize you can't actually answer without running it.

contentSections.scenario: Two different feelings while reading unfamiliar code: (A) "I recognize this syntax and roughly what kind of thing it's doing" — a fast, shallow read. (B) "I could predict what this returns for a specific input, including an edge case, without running it" — a slower, deeper check.
contentSections.question: Which of these actually tells you it's safe to change this code?

options.label: B — being able to predict its behavior for a real input, including an edge case, is a genuine test of understanding, not just familiarity
A — recognizing the syntax is enough; unfamiliar syntax is the real risk, not unfamiliar logic
Neither — you can never really know if you understand code you didn't write

feedback.b: Right. Recognizing .filter() and .map() as familiar syntax tells you almost nothing about what *this specific* function does with *this specific* data — being able to predict a real output, especially for an edge case, is what actually demonstrates understanding, and it's a check you can run on yourself before making a change.
feedback.a: Recognizing syntax is real, but shallow — you can recognize every symbol in a sentence in a language you don't actually speak. The risk in unfamiliar code is almost always in the specific logic, not in whether the syntax looks familiar.
feedback.neither: You can absolutely build real understanding of code you didn't write — that's most of what a working developer does. The point isn't that it's unknowable, it's that recognizing syntax isn't the same test as actually being able to predict behavior.

contentSections.concept: Recognizing code — the syntax looks familiar, the general shape makes sense — is a shallow, fast read. Understanding code — being able to predict what it does for a specific input, including an edge case, without running it — is a deeper, slower check, and it's the one that actually predicts whether you can change the code safely.

contentSections.body: This distinction matters because recognizing feels like understanding from the inside — there's no obvious internal signal telling you "this is shallow." The only way to actually check is to deliberately test yourself: pick a real input (ideally an edge case, per the testing module) and try to predict the output before running the code. If you can't, that's real information — not a failure, just an honest signal that more reading (or asking) is needed before changing this particular piece.
Recognizing syntax feels like understanding from the inside, but it isn't — being able to predict a real, specific output is the actual test.

contentSections.title: What to do once you know you don't understand it yet

contentSections.body: You try to predict what a function returns for an empty cart and can't. That's useful information — the question is what to actually do with it, rather than either faking confidence or giving up.

contentSections.question: You've honestly determined you don't yet understand a piece of code well enough to change it safely. Is the right move to guess anyway and see what happens, or to do something else first?
contentSections.hint: You already have real tools from this module for closing exactly this kind of gap.
contentSections.answer: Something else first — this is exactly the situation the rest of this module built tools for: trace the specific thread you're unsure about (lesson 2), jump to the real definition of anything you're guessing at (lesson 3), or run the specific input you couldn't predict and see what actually happens, treating that as a deliberate experiment rather than a blind guess in production. "I don't understand this yet" is a normal, common, entirely fixable state — not a stopping point, and not a reason to fake confidence and change code you can't actually predict.

contentSections.body: Not understanding a piece of code yet is normal and fixable — trace it, jump to its real definition, or test a prediction deliberately, rather than guessing or freezing.

description: Eight drills, no new concepts: given a described unfamiliar project or piece of code, apply this module's approach to finding, tracing, and safely changing it.

learningObjectives.text: Apply orientation, tracing, search, and safe-change practices to a described unfamiliar codebase

contentSections.title: Eight scenarios, the standard from this module

contentSections.body: Every one of these traces back to something from this module: starting from the entry point instead of reading everything, following one concrete thread, searching by specific identifiers, jump-to-definition over guessing from a name, scoping a change small, verifying it properly, and telling recognition apart from real understanding.
The same real question every time: what's the smallest, most specific thread you can actually follow to the answer, instead of trying to read everything?

title: Lab — Make One Change to a Project You Didn't Write
description: Find a real, unfamiliar project — someone else's, or an old one of your own you've genuinely forgotten — and make one real, small, verified change to it, writing down exactly how you found where to make it.

learningObjectives.text: Orient in an unfamiliar codebase using its README and entry point
Trace a specific behavior to the code responsible for it
Make and verify a small, safely scoped change

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Find a project you didn't write, or one of your own from long enough ago that it genuinely feels unfamiliar — an open-source project's small repo, a classmate's, or an old project of yours you've forgotten the details of. By the end of this lab, you'll have made one real, verified change to it and written an honest account of how you found where to make it.

contentSections.title: Make one change to a project you didn't write
contentSections.brief: Choose an unfamiliar project of reasonable size (a small open-source repo, or an old project you've genuinely forgotten). Identify one small, concrete change worth making — a real bug, a small missing feature, or an improvement — and make it, using this module's approach to find where it belongs and verify it's actually correct.
contentSections.deliverable: A working change plus a written account of how you found where to make it.

stages.title: Orient
stages.instructions: Read the project's README (or write down what you can infer if there isn't one) and find its entry point. Skim what the entry point calls, just enough to see the overall shape, without chasing every branch yet.
stages.checkpoint: You can describe, in a few sentences, what this project does and roughly how it's organized, without having read every file.

stages.title: Choose and trace
stages.instructions: Pick one specific, concrete thing to change — a real bug you find, or a small feature genuinely worth adding. Trace it to the exact code responsible, using search by specific identifiers and jump-to-definition rather than reading files top to bottom.
stages.checkpoint: You can point to the exact line(s) responsible, and explain the specific search or trace steps that led you there.

stages.title: Make the smallest change that fixes it
stages.instructions: Make the change, scoped to only what's needed for the one thing you identified — not a wider cleanup of anything else you noticed along the way (write those down separately if you want to remember them).
stages.checkpoint: The change is scoped to exactly the one issue, with any other noticed issues written down but not touched.

stages.title: Verify it, honestly
stages.instructions: Run the specific case you fixed and confirm it now behaves correctly. Run at least one case that should NOT trigger the fixed behavior, and confirm it still doesn't. If the project has an existing test suite, run it.
stages.checkpoint: You've actually run (not just read) the fixed case, a case that shouldn't be affected, and the existing tests if any exist.

rubric.criterion: Orientation used the entry point, not blind reading
rubric.meets: You can describe the project's shape from its README and entry point, without having read every file top to bottom.

rubric.criterion: The trace to the relevant code is specific and explainable
rubric.meets: You can name the exact search terms or jump-to-definition steps that led to the responsible code.

rubric.criterion: The change is scoped to one thing
rubric.meets: Nothing beyond the identified issue was touched, even if other issues were noticed.

rubric.criterion: The change was actually verified, not just read
rubric.meets: The fixed case, a non-triggering case, and any existing tests were actually run, not just visually checked.

rubric.criterion: The written account is honest and specific
rubric.meets: It describes the real search/trace process used, including any dead ends — not a cleaned-up version that skips the actual reasoning.

contentSections.body: A real, working change to code you didn't write — with an honest account of how you actually found it — is the whole point of this module, and it's a genuinely learnable skill, not something only experienced developers can do.

title: Checkpoint — Reading Other People's Code
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Organising a Project, two reaching back into Version Control and Checking Your Own Work. Ungraded, untimed.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's core distinctions, and earlier ones, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Reading Other People's Code

questions.from: This module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: Why is a project's entry point a better place to start reading than the file explorer's alphabetical order?

options.label: It's the one place everything the program does actually starts from, so following what it calls builds a real map of how pieces connect
The entry point is always the shortest file in the project
Alphabetical order is only a problem in very large projects

questions.explanation: File-explorer order has no relationship to how code actually runs. The entry point is guaranteed to matter because everything the program does starts from there.

questions.from: This module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: Do you need to fully understand every file in an unfamiliar project before making one specific fix?

options.label: No — following the one specific thread the fix actually touches is the real, bounded skill
Yes — any change risks breaking something you haven't read
Only for projects under 500 lines

questions.explanation: Most real changes touch a small fraction of a project — tracing the specific thread that matters is the actual, learnable skill, not full comprehension of everything.

questions.from: This module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: Why is searching for a specific function name usually better than searching for a generic word like "discount"?

options.label: A specific identifier narrows results to what's actually relevant, where a generic word returns comments and unrelated code too
Generic words are not supported by most code search tools
There's no real difference in practice

questions.explanation: A specific, rare identifier returns a small, relevant result set. Generic words return everything loosely related, which is nearly as unhelpful as no search at all.

questions.from: This module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: What's the actual test of whether you understand a piece of unfamiliar code, versus just recognizing its syntax?

options.label: Being able to predict what it returns for a specific real input, including an edge case, without running it
Being able to read it out loud fluently
Recognizing every keyword and symbol used in it

questions.explanation: Recognizing familiar syntax is shallow — predicting real behavior for a specific input is the deeper check that actually indicates understanding.

questions.from: Previous module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: From Organising a Project: what's the actual sign a single-file project has outgrown that structure?

options.label: A pointable cost — scrolling past unrelated code, tangled features, or colliding changes
Reaching a specific line-count threshold
Having been open for more than a month

questions.explanation: The real signal is a concrete friction you can point to, not a size threshold on its own.

questions.from: Previous module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: From Organising a Project: why does splitting a file into part1.js/part2.js/part3.js by line count often fail to actually help?

options.label: Related code can still be scattered across all three files — only splitting by responsibility groups it usefully
It doesn't fail — any split into smaller files is always an improvement
JavaScript doesn't support more than two files in a project

questions.explanation: A split by arbitrary boundary doesn't group related code together — it just spreads the same tangle across more files.

questions.from: Previous module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: From Organising a Project: why does a hardcoded localhost URL break once a project is deployed?

options.label: localhost means "this machine" — correct locally, meaningless once the code runs elsewhere
fetch() itself stops functioning after deployment
The URL becomes invalid syntax once deployed

questions.explanation: The value is genuinely correct in exactly one environment — configuration exists to let it change per environment without touching the code.

questions.from: Previous module — Organising a Project
questions.prompt: From Organising a Project: what makes a README's setup section actually useful, beyond describing what the project does?

options.label: Exact, specific install/configure/run instructions that can't be guessed from a general description
A longer explanation of why the project was built
Listing every function in the codebase

questions.explanation: A description explains what a project is; specific setup steps are what actually let a stranger run this particular project.

questions.from: Three modules back — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: why is git revert safer than rewriting history for a commit that's already been shared?

options.label: Revert adds a new corrective commit instead of rewriting shared history, so everyone's copy stays in sync
Revert is simply faster to type than the alternatives
There's no real difference between the two

questions.explanation: Rewriting a commit someone else already has creates disagreeing versions of "the same" commit — revert avoids that by never rewriting shared history.

questions.from: Four modules back — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: what's the concrete way to prove a test would actually catch a real bug?

options.label: Temporarily break the code it tests and confirm the test fails, then revert and confirm it passes again
Check that the test has a long, detailed name
Run the test suite twice in a row

questions.explanation: Watching a test go red on deliberately broken code, then green again on the real code, is the actual proof it checks something meaningful.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Reproduce it reliably before you fix anything
description: A bug you can't reliably make happen again is a bug you can't actually confirm you've fixed — reproduction comes before any attempt at a fix, every time.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why fixing a bug before reliably reproducing it risks a fix that doesn't actually work
Identify the specific steps that make a bug happen, as a first debugging move

contentSections.title: You can't know you fixed it if you can't make it happen

contentSections.body: A user reports: "sometimes the save button doesn't work." You open the app, click save a few times, it works every time. You make a guess at what might be wrong, change something, and ship it. The user reports the bug again three days later — your "fix" changed something, but not the actual cause, because you never actually saw the bug happen yourself.

contentSections.scenario: Two approaches to "sometimes the save button doesn't work": (A) guess at likely causes, change something that seems reasonable, and ship it. (B) find the exact, specific steps that make the bug happen reliably, confirm you can trigger it on demand, then make a change and confirm those same steps no longer trigger it.
contentSections.question: Which approach actually tells you, with confidence, that the bug is fixed?

options.label: B — only by reliably making the bug happen, then confirming the same steps no longer cause it, can you actually know something specific was fixed
A — a reasonable-sounding fix is enough, since the bug clearly involves the save button
Neither — some bugs are genuinely unknowable and unfixable

feedback.b: Right. Without a reliable way to trigger the bug, "is it fixed?" has no real answer — you're just hoping. Once you can make it happen on demand, a fix is testable: run the same steps, and either the bug is gone or it isn't, with real evidence either way.
feedback.a: A change can be reasonable, related to the right area, and still not address the actual cause — without ever having reproduced the bug, there's no way to confirm the change did anything except make it *feel* handled.
feedback.neither: Almost every bug is reproducible with enough specific detail about the conditions that trigger it — "sometimes" almost always means "under conditions I haven't identified yet," not "unknowable." Finding those conditions is exactly what this lesson is about.

contentSections.concept: A bug you can't reliably reproduce is a bug you can't confirm you've fixed — any change you make is a guess you have no way to verify. Reproduction always comes first: find the specific, repeatable steps that trigger the bug, confirm you can make it happen on demand, and only then start looking for the cause.

contentSections.body: "Sometimes" is rarely truly random — it usually means "under some specific condition I haven't identified yet." Getting from "sometimes" to "reliably" means asking concrete questions: does it happen on every browser, or one specific one? Every time, or only with a particular kind of input (an empty field, a very long one)? Only after a specific sequence of other actions? Each answer narrows "sometimes" toward a specific, repeatable trigger — the actual starting point for any real debugging.
"Sometimes" usually means "under a specific condition you haven't found yet" — finding that condition is what turns an unfixable-feeling bug into a reproducible, fixable one.

contentSections.title: Write down the exact steps, every time

contentSections.body: You finally get the save bug to happen — after clicking save with an empty title field. You fix it, but don't write the steps down. Two weeks later a similar bug is reported, and you can't remember if it was the empty title, or something else about that specific sequence, that actually caused it.

contentSections.question: You've found the exact steps that reliably trigger a bug. Is it worth the extra minute to write them down as a numbered list before starting to look for the cause?
contentSections.hint: Think about what you'd need if the first fix attempt doesn't actually work, or if a similar bug shows up later.
contentSections.answer: Yes — a written, numbered reproduction ("1. Open the form. 2. Leave the title field empty. 3. Click save.") is what lets you re-check quickly after any change, hand the exact steps to someone else, or compare a future bug report against this one to see if it's actually the same issue. Without it, reproducing the bug again after a failed fix attempt means re-discovering the same steps from scratch, which is exactly the kind of avoidable, repeated work this module is trying to remove.

contentSections.body: This is a small habit with a large payoff: the moment you can reliably make a bug happen, write the exact steps down, in order, specific enough that someone else (or you, in a week) could follow them exactly and get the same result. It costs a minute and saves much more than a minute the first time a fix attempt doesn't actually work and you need to re-verify from scratch.
Write down the exact reproduction steps the moment you find them — it's the cheapest insurance against re-discovering them later.

title: Narrowing down: halving the search space
description: Instead of guessing where a bug lives, deliberately check the midpoint of the code the bug could possibly be in, and eliminate half the possibilities with each check — the same idea as looking up a word in a paper dictionary.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a binary-search approach to narrow down where in a sequence of code a bug is introduced

contentSections.title: Check the middle, not the start

contentSections.body: A function runs ten steps in a row — validate input, calculate a subtotal, apply a discount, add tax, round, format, and so on — and the final output is wrong. The instinct is to start at step one and check every single step in order until something looks off.

contentSections.problem: A ten-step calculation produces the wrong final number. Find which step first goes wrong, without checking all ten in order.

steps.label: Check the midpoint first, not the start
steps.work: Print (or inspect) the value after step 5 of 10.
steps.why: Checking the middle first, rather than starting at step 1, immediately splits the problem in half: if step 5's value is already wrong, the bug is in steps 1-5; if it's still correct, the bug is in steps 6-10.

steps.label: Suppose step 5's value is correct — narrow to the second half
steps.work: Print the value after step 8 (the midpoint of steps 6-10).
steps.why: The bug must be in steps 6-10, so checking their midpoint (step 8) again cuts the remaining possibilities in half, exactly the same idea applied again.

steps.label: Suppose step 8 is wrong — narrow to steps 6-8
steps.work: Print the value after step 7 (the midpoint of steps 6-8).
steps.why: One more halving: the bug is now known to be in step 7 or step 8, since step 6 (implicitly, being before 7) hasn't been ruled in or out yet — check step 6 next if needed, but the search space is already down to 2-3 candidates from an original 10.

steps.label: Confirm the exact step
steps.work: Compare step 7's expected value (calculated by hand) to what the code actually produced.
steps.why: At this point you're checking one specific step's logic directly, not searching anymore — the halving process did its job of narrowing ten candidates down to one.

faded.problem: A different function runs eight sequential transformations on a dataset, and the final result is wrong. Narrow down which transformation introduces the error.

blanks.prompt: First check — which step's output do you inspect first?
blanks.why: Checking the midpoint first splits eight candidates into two groups of four in a single check, rather than checking from the start.

blanks.prompt: If step 4's output is already wrong, where's the bug narrowed to?
blanks.why: A wrong value at step 4 means the error was introduced at or before that point — the second half (5-8) is ruled out entirely.

blanks.prompt: What's the next check, to narrow steps 1-4 further?
blanks.why: Repeating the same halving logic on the remaining half is what keeps cutting the search space down with each check, rather than checking every remaining step one by one.

contentSections.procedure: Check the midpoint of the range the bug could be in, use the result to eliminate half the remaining possibilities, and repeat on the remaining half — narrowing a long sequence to one specific step in a handful of checks instead of checking every step in order.

contentSections.body: Checking the midpoint of where a bug could be, and repeating on whichever half remains, narrows a long sequence down far faster than checking from the start.

contentSections.title: This works on more than sequential steps

contentSections.body: The same halving idea applies beyond a linear sequence of steps — it works on git history too, and on a long list of recent changes when you don't know which one introduced a bug.

contentSections.scenario: A bug is discovered that definitely wasn't there 50 commits ago, and definitely is there now. Checking all 50 commits one at a time, in order, would take 50 checks in the worst case.
contentSections.question: Applying the same halving idea from this lesson, roughly how many checks does it take to find the exact commit that introduced the bug, in the worst case?

options.label: About 6 — checking the midpoint commit each time and discarding half the remaining range, the same way a 10-step search narrowed to one step in about 4 checks
Still 50 — halving only works on sequential code steps, not on commit history
1 — the halving approach finds the exact commit immediately every time

feedback.log_n: Right. Each check (does this commit have the bug or not?) cuts the remaining range in half, regardless of whether you're checking calculation steps or commits — 50 candidates becomes 25, then about 12, 6, 3, 1, in roughly 6 checks total. This exact approach, applied to git history, is what a tool like `git bisect` automates.
feedback.still_50: The halving logic doesn't care what's being narrowed — steps in a calculation, commits in history, lines in a file — it only needs a way to check "is the bug present at this point or not," which works identically for a commit as it does for a calculation step.
feedback.one: Each individual check only cuts the space in half, not down to one — it takes several checks in sequence (roughly the number of times you can halve 50 before reaching 1) to actually pin down the exact source.

contentSections.mechanism: Halving works on anything that can be checked at a specific point and ordered — sequential code steps, a range of commits, a long list. Each check eliminates half the remaining possibilities, which is why it takes only a handful of checks even for a large search space, dramatically fewer than checking everything one at a time.

contentSections.body: The same halving idea works on anything checkable and ordered — steps, commits, a long list — turning dozens of possible checks into a handful.

title: Printing values versus using a debugger
description: Printing a value at a specific point is fast and low-setup; a real debugger lets you pause execution and inspect everything at that moment — each is the right tool for a different kind of situation.

learningObjectives.text: Choose between a print statement and a debugger for a given debugging situation
Set a breakpoint and inspect a variable's value at that point

contentSections.title: Two real tools, not one "correct" one

contentSections.body: You want to know what a variable equals right before a crash. One option: add `console.log(myVariable)` right there, run it, read the output. Another: set a breakpoint at that exact line, run it, and the program actually pauses there, letting you inspect not just that one variable but everything currently in scope.

contentSections.scenario: Two debugging tools: printing (console.log at a specific point, then re-running) and a debugger (a breakpoint that pauses real execution at that point, letting you inspect any variable, step forward one line at a time, and see the full call stack).
contentSections.question: You want to check one specific variable's value at one specific point, in a small script, just once. Which is the faster, more proportionate tool?

options.label: A print statement — fast to add, no setup, perfectly adequate for checking one known thing at one known point
A debugger — always the more thorough choice, so it's always worth the extra setup
Neither is appropriate for a small script — small scripts should be debugged by re-reading the code

feedback.print: Right. For checking one known value at one known point, a print statement is genuinely the more proportionate tool — it's immediate, needs no setup, and answers exactly the question you have. Reaching for a debugger's full pause-and-inspect machinery for a single known check is more tool than the situation calls for.
feedback.debugger: A debugger is more powerful, but more powerful isn't automatically better for every situation — for one known variable at one known point, the extra setup (finding the line, setting the breakpoint, starting a debug session) costs more than it returns here.
feedback.neither: Re-reading code can reveal some bugs, but it can't tell you what a variable actually equals at runtime — that requires either printing the value or pausing execution to inspect it, exactly what these two tools are for.

contentSections.concept: A print statement is fast and low-setup — ideal when you know roughly what you're looking for and just need to confirm a specific value at a specific point. A debugger is more powerful and more expensive to set up — ideal when you don't yet know what you're looking for and need to explore the full state of the program, step through execution, or inspect several things at once at a point you're not certain about in advance.

contentSections.body: A rough rule of thumb: reach for a print statement when you have a specific hypothesis ("I think x is the wrong value right here") and just want to confirm or deny it quickly. Reach for a debugger when you're exploring — you don't yet know which variable is wrong, you want to step through execution one line at a time and watch things change, or you need to see several values and the call stack together at once, which would mean adding and then removing a pile of separate print statements.
A print statement answers one specific, known question fast. A debugger is worth its extra setup when you're exploring, not yet sure what you're looking for.

contentSections.title: Setting a breakpoint and actually looking

contentSections.body: You set a breakpoint at the line where a discount is calculated, run the code, and it actually pauses there — mid-execution, frozen, everything currently in scope inspectable, before that line has even run.

contentSections.question: You set a breakpoint on the line `const finalPrice = price - (price * percent / 100);` and run the code. At the moment execution pauses there, has that line already run?
contentSections.hint: A breakpoint pauses execution right before the line it's set on actually runs.
contentSections.answer: No — a breakpoint pauses execution just before that line runs, which is exactly what makes it useful: you can inspect price and percent's current values right at that moment, before finalPrice is calculated, to check whether the inputs going into the calculation are already what you expect. If they're already wrong at this point, the bug is upstream of this line; if they're correct, the bug is in this specific calculation or after it.

contentSections.body: From a paused breakpoint, the real value is what you can do next: inspect any variable currently in scope, not just the one you were watching for; step forward one line at a time and watch values change in real time; and see the full call stack — exactly which functions called which, in order, to get to this exact point. This is the kind of exploration that would take a large, awkward pile of print statements to approximate, and a debugger does it live, without editing the code at all.
A breakpoint pauses execution right before its line runs, giving you a live, explorable snapshot — the full call stack and every variable in scope, not just the one you were watching for.

title: The bug that's in your assumption, not your code
description: Some bugs live in code you never look at because you're certain it's fine — the actual cause is an assumption that's silently wrong, not a mistake you can find by rereading code you already trust.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when a debugging dead end is caused by an unchecked assumption rather than the code being examined

contentSections.title: You've read this line ten times because you're sure it's fine

contentSections.body: A function that sorts a list of orders by date is producing an out-of-order result. You've re-read the sorting logic six times — it's correct, textbook correct. What you never checked: whether the dates coming in are actually Date objects, or strings that only *look* sortable.

contentSections.question: The sort logic itself is textbook-correct for real Date objects or numeric timestamps. Given the actual data being passed in here, what's the real problem?

options.label: date is a string, not a Date object or a number — subtracting two strings doesn't compare them chronologically the way the code assumes
The sort() method itself is broken
The array needs to have exactly 3 items to sort correctly

feedback.assumption: Right. `a.date - b.date` assumes date is something subtraction produces a meaningful chronological difference for — true for real Date objects or numeric timestamps, false for a plain string. The sorting *logic* is genuinely correct; the *assumption* about what kind of value date actually is turned out to be wrong, which is exactly the kind of bug re-reading the sort logic alone would never catch.
feedback.sort_broken: sort() itself works exactly as documented — it's being handed a comparison function that makes a false assumption about its inputs, not a broken built-in method.
feedback.length: Array length has nothing to do with this — the problem is entirely about what kind of value date actually is, regardless of how many items are being sorted.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This is the specific trap this lesson is about: rereading code you're already confident is correct, over and over, while the actual bug is in an assumption about the data feeding into it — here, that date is already a sortable type, when it's actually a plain string. The fix (converting the strings to real Date objects before sorting, or comparing them differently) lives outside the code being stared at.

contentSections.body: Rereading code you're confident is correct, again and again, doesn't help when the actual bug is in an unchecked assumption about what's feeding into it.

contentSections.title: Question the thing you're most sure about

contentSections.body: After enough time stuck on a bug, staring at code that seems obviously fine, a useful — if uncomfortable — move is to deliberately question the single thing you're most certain isn't the problem.

contentSections.scenario: Genuinely stuck on a bug after reading the suspected code repeatedly with no luck. Candidate next moves: keep rereading the same lines more carefully; print or inspect the actual value and type of an input you've been assuming is correct; assume the bug is unsolvable and work around it elsewhere; deliberately question the one assumption you're most confident about.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely productive next moves when stuck? Select all that apply.

items.label: Print or inspect the actual value and type of an input you've been assuming is correct
Deliberately question the one assumption you're most confident about — the thing you'd never think to check
Keep rereading the same lines even more carefully, for the seventh time
Assume the bug is unsolvable and quietly work around it elsewhere in the code

explanation.print_input: Checking the actual runtime value and type of something you've assumed is correct is exactly how the date-as-string bug above would be caught — it tests the assumption directly instead of trusting it.
explanation.question_assumption: This is the deliberate version of the same idea: after several failed attempts on the code itself, the highest-value move is often questioning the thing you're most sure about, precisely because that's the one place you haven't actually looked.
explanation.reread_more: If six careful readings haven't found anything, a seventh read of the same lines is unlikely to either — the problem usually isn't a lack of attention on the code, it's that the bug isn't in the code being read at all.
explanation.workaround: A silent workaround hides the symptom without understanding the cause — it also means the same wrong assumption is still sitting there, ready to cause a different, harder-to-connect bug somewhere else later.

contentSections.body: When rereading trusted code repeatedly isn't working, the highest-value move is often checking the one assumption you're most confident about — that's usually the actual blind spot.

title: Writing a test that captures the bug
description: Once a bug is found and fixed, a test built from the exact reproduction steps makes sure it can never silently come back — turning a one-time fix into a permanent, automated guarantee.

learningObjectives.text: Write a regression test from a bug's reproduction steps
Explain why fixing a bug without a regression test leaves it able to recur silently

contentSections.title: A fix without a test can quietly come back

contentSections.body: You found and fixed the date-sorting bug from lesson 4 — dates are now converted to real Date objects before sorting. Two months later, someone refactors that code, accidentally reintroduces the same string-comparison mistake, and nothing catches it. The bug is back, silently, exactly like it never got fixed at all.

contentSections.question: You fixed a real bug but never wrote a test for it. Six months later, an unrelated refactor accidentally reintroduces the exact same bug. Does anything automatically catch this?
contentSections.hint: This connects directly back to the testing module — what does an automated test actually protect against?
contentSections.answer: No — without a test specifically covering this case, nothing runs automatically to notice the bug came back. The fix only lives in the current code; if a later change (even an unrelated one) reverts that specific logic, there's no automated check to catch it, exactly the regression problem the testing module introduced. This is the entire reason a fix and a regression test go together: the fix solves it now, the test keeps it solved.

contentSections.body: A regression test is built directly from the bug's own reproduction steps — the exact input that used to trigger the bug becomes the test's input, and the correct behavior (the fix) becomes the expected result. For the date bug: `expect(sortByDate([{date: '2024-3-1'}, {date: '2024-1-15'}])).toEqual([{date: '2024-1-15'}, {date: '2024-3-1'}]);` — using the real dates that actually exposed the bug, not a simplified, easier example that might not exercise the same code path.
A fix without a regression test only solves the bug right now — a test built from the real reproduction steps is what keeps it solved.

contentSections.title: This is the loop the whole module has been building

contentSections.body: Reproduce reliably, narrow down with halving, inspect with prints or a debugger, question the assumption if stuck, fix it — and then, the step that closes the loop and connects straight back to the testing module.

contentSections.question: Put the full debugging loop this module has built, start to finish, in order:
steps: Find the exact, specific steps that reliably reproduce the bug
Narrow down where the bug lives, halving the search space rather than checking everything in order
Inspect the relevant values with a print statement or a debugger to confirm the actual cause
Fix the code (checking any assumption that turned out to be wrong, not just the visible logic)
Write a regression test built from the original reproduction steps, and confirm it fails on the old, broken code and passes on the fix
contentSections.explanation: This is the full loop: reproduce, narrow, inspect, fix, and lock the fix in place with a regression test — verified, per the testing module, by confirming the test actually fails on the broken version before trusting that it passes on the fixed one. Skipping the last step means the fix is real but temporary; skipping the first means every later step is built on a guess about what's even happening.

contentSections.body: Reproduce, narrow, inspect, fix, and lock it in with a regression test — this is the full loop, and skipping the last step leaves even a correct fix able to silently unravel.

questions.from: This module — Debugging Properly
questions.prompt: Why does making a fix before reliably reproducing a bug risk shipping a fix that doesn't actually work?

options.label: Without a reliable way to trigger the bug, there's no way to confirm the change actually addressed the real cause rather than something unrelated
It doesn't risk anything — a reasonable-looking fix is generally enough
The risk is only that it takes longer, not that it might not work

questions.explanation: A bug you can't reliably reproduce is a bug you can't confirm you've fixed — the change is a guess with no way to verify it addressed the real cause.

questions.from: This module — Debugging Properly
questions.prompt: Roughly how many checks does halving the search space take to find one bad step among 50, compared to checking each one in order?

options.label: About 6 checks, versus up to 50 checking one at a time
Exactly the same number of checks either way
It only works for sequences of exactly 10 or fewer

questions.explanation: Each check eliminates half the remaining possibilities, so 50 candidates narrow to 1 in roughly 6 checks — dramatically fewer than checking every one in order.

questions.from: This module — Debugging Properly
questions.prompt: A sort function's logic is textbook-correct, but the result is still wrong. What's the more productive next move after several careful re-reads find nothing?

options.label: Check the actual value and type of the data feeding into it — the bug may be in an unchecked assumption, not the logic itself
Reread the same logic even more carefully
Assume the built-in sort function itself is broken

questions.explanation: Rereading code you're already confident is correct rarely helps when the real bug is a wrong assumption about the data feeding into it, like a string being treated as a sortable value.

questions.from: This module — Debugging Properly
questions.prompt: Why does a bug fix need a regression test, not just the fix itself?

options.label: Without a test, a later unrelated change could silently reintroduce the same bug with nothing automatically catching it
A regression test is only needed if the bug was especially hard to find
The fix alone is always sufficient — a test is a nice-to-have, not a real need

questions.explanation: A fix without a test only solves the bug right now — a regression test, built from the real reproduction steps, is what keeps it solved against future changes.

questions.from: Previous module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: From Reading Other People's Code: why is a project's entry point a better place to start than reading files in alphabetical order?

options.label: It's the one place everything the program does actually starts from, so following what it calls builds a real map
The entry point is always the shortest file
Alphabetical order only matters in very large projects

questions.explanation: File-explorer order has no relationship to how code actually runs — the entry point is guaranteed to matter because every run starts there.

questions.from: Previous module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: From Reading Other People's Code: what's the actual test of understanding a piece of unfamiliar code, beyond recognizing its syntax?

options.label: Being able to predict its output for a specific real input, including an edge case, without running it
Being able to read it aloud fluently
Recognizing every keyword it uses

questions.explanation: Recognizing familiar syntax is shallow — predicting real behavior for a specific input is the deeper check that actually indicates understanding.

questions.from: Previous module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: From Reading Other People's Code: why is jump-to-definition more reliable than guessing a function's behavior from its name?

options.label: A function's actual behavior, including any side effects, is only reliably found in its real, current code — names can be incomplete or outdated
Names are always accurate, but jump-to-definition is simply faster
It isn't more reliable — names are always sufficient in well-written code

questions.explanation: Names are written by people and can drift from what the code actually does — the real definition is the only reliable source of truth.

questions.from: Previous module — Reading Other People's Code
questions.prompt: From Reading Other People's Code: what's the safer scope for a change in code you don't yet fully understand?

options.label: The smallest change that fixes the one thing you were asked about, with other noticed issues written down separately
Fixing everything you notice at once, since you're already in the file
No change at all, until you understand the entire codebase

questions.explanation: Each unrelated change bundled in is an additional risk in code you don't yet fully understand, and makes any resulting bug harder to isolate.

questions.from: Three modules back — Checking Your Own Work
questions.prompt: From Checking Your Own Work: what's the concrete way to prove a test would actually catch a real bug?

options.label: Temporarily break the code it tests and confirm the test fails, then revert and confirm it passes again
Give the test a longer, more detailed name
Run the same test twice in a row

questions.explanation: Watching a test go red on deliberately broken code, then green again on the real code, is the actual proof it checks something meaningful.

questions.from: Four modules back — Version Control
questions.prompt: From Version Control: what does `git reset --hard` do to uncommitted changes in the working directory?

options.label: Discards them, related or not, with no automatic backup
Leaves them completely untouched
Automatically commits them before resetting

questions.explanation: "Hard" forces the working directory to match the target commit, silently discarding any uncommitted work in its path.
